game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Fair value before any reveal is 10.5, the expected sum of three dice. I compared half-spreads by weighing expected profit from noise traders (65%, valuation noise with standard deviation 4.4) against expected loss to informed traders (35%), using the exact distribution of the dice sum.

| Half-spread | Expected net per side |
|---|---|
| 2.0 | about 0.26 |
| 3.0 | about 0.40 |
| 3.5 | about 0.43 |
| 4.0 | about 0.43 |

The curve is flat between 3.5 and 4, so I'm quoting about ±3.7 around 10.5.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 14.2}

Before any dice are revealed, the fair value is 10.5 (three dice at 3.5 each). I looked at the expected profit on each side for a range of half-spreads. A noise trader pays me roughly the half-spread when it trades. An informed trader takes me only when the settlement value is beyond my price.

| Half-spread | Gain from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net per side |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0 | 0.42 | 0.16 | 0.26 |
| 3.0 | 0.48 | 0.09 | 0.40 |
| 3.5 | 0.48 | 0.06 | 0.43 |
| 4.0 | 0.47 | 0.04 | 0.43 |

The net profit is roughly flat between half-spreads of 3.5 and 4. The last quote (half-spread 3.7) got no trade, which tells me very little about the dice. I'll quote a half-spread of 3.5, symmetric around 10.5.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 14.0}

Fair value is 11: the revealed die 1 is 4, and the two unrevealed dice average 7.

Each side of the quote is a trade-off. Noise traders give me an edge, while informed traders pick me off when the remaining two dice land far from 7.

I priced a half-spread h on one side as the noise profit minus the informed loss:
- **h ≈ 2.5:** expected profit about +0.40 per side.
- **h ≈ 3.5:** about +0.46 per side.
- **h ≈ 4:** about +0.46 per side.

The optimum is around 3.5 to 4, so I'll quote a half-spread of 3.7.

{"bid": 7.3, "ask": 14.7}

Die 1 is revealed as 4, and the other two dice each average 3.5. That puts fair value at **11**. The value can range from 6 to 16. None of the earlier quotes traded, but that tells us little because the information is symmetric.

To pick the spread, I compared expected edge per side against the half-spread (h):
- **Noise traders (probability 0.65):** I earn h × P(noise > h), with noise standard deviation 4.4.
- **Informed traders (probability 0.35):** I lose the amount the true value exceeds my ask, which only happens on high totals of the two remaining dice.

| h | Ask | Expected edge per side |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 13 | ≈ 0.33 |
| 3 | 14 | ≈ 0.44 |
| 3.5 | 14.5 | ≈ 0.46 |
| 4 | 15 | ≈ 0.46 |

The edge is roughly flat between h = 3.5 and h = 4, so I quote about 3.6 either side of 11, giving 7.4 / 14.6.

{"bid": 7.4, "ask": 14.6}

With dice 1 and 2 revealed (4 + 6 = 10), only die 3 is unknown. The fair value is 13.5, and the contract can only settle between 11 and 16.

**Ask side.** An informed counterparty buys only when the settlement value is above my ask. Any ask of 16 or higher is therefore never hit by an informed trader, so only noise traders buy there. Noise traders value the contract at 13.5 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 4.4. The expected profit from the ask is 0.65 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 13.5):

| Ask | Chance a noise trader buys | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|
| 16 | about 0.285 | about 0.46 |
| 16.5 | about 0.248 | about 0.48 |
| 17 | about 0.213 | about 0.485 |
| 17.5 | about 0.182 | about 0.47 |

The best ask is about 17.

**Bid side.** The setup is symmetric around 13.5. Any bid of 11 or lower is never hit by an informed trader, and the same calculation gives a best bid of about 10.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 17}

Fair value is 13.5 (dice 1 and 2 sum to 10, plus 3.5 expected from die 3). Every possible settlement lies between 11 and 16.

- **Ask side:** Any ask at 16 or above loses nothing to informed traders, because no settlement value is above it. Against noise traders, the expected edge per quote is 0.65 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 13.5). This peaks at an ask of about 16.8–17.0, giving roughly 0.49 per quote.
- **Bid side:** By symmetry, the best bid is about 10.2. Informed traders never sell below that, since the lowest possible settlement is 11.

{"bid": 10.2, "ask": 16.8}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Fair value is 10.5, the expected sum of three dice. Before any reveal, the sum has a standard deviation of about 2.96.

I compared half-spreads around fair value. For each one I set the noise-trader profit against the expected loss to informed traders:

| Half-spread | Ask | Noise profit | Informed loss | Net per side |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 13.5 | ≈ 0.48 | ≈ 0.085 | ≈ 0.40 |
| 3.5 | 14 | ≈ 0.49 | ≈ 0.06 | ≈ 0.43 |
| 4 | 14.5 | ≈ 0.47 | ≈ 0.04 | ≈ 0.43 |

A half-spread of 3.5 to 4 is about the best, so I'll quote 7 / 14. The distribution is symmetric, so the bid side works out the same way.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 14.0}

The public fair value has dropped from 10.5 to about 9.5, so I'll quote 7.4 / 11.4 around it.

**Updating fair value after the first trade.** Before any trades, the expected sum of three dice is 10.5, with a standard deviation of about 2.96. A counterparty then sold to me at 7. There are two ways that happens:

- **Informed seller:** this happens only if the true sum is 6 or less.
  - That has probability 20/216 ≈ 0.093.
  - Weighted by the 0.35 chance of an informed trader, this gives about 0.032.
  - If the sum is 6 or less, its average is 5.25.
- **Noise seller:** this happens if their valuation fell below 7.
  - Their valuation is centred on 10.5 with standard deviation 4.4, so this has probability about 0.21.
  - Weighted by the 0.65 chance of a noise trader, this gives about 0.139.
  - A noise sale tells me nothing about the true sum, so its average stays 10.5.

Combining the two, the posterior mean is (0.032 × 5.25 + 0.139 × 10.5) / 0.171 ≈ 9.5.

**Setting the quote.** I keep the spread at about ±2 around 9.5 to guard against informed traders. I skew it slightly down because I am already long one unit.

{"bid": 7.4, "ask": 11.4}

Fair value is about 12.7, and I'm quoting 10.9 / 14.5 around it.

**Estimating fair value.** Die 1 is 5, so the sum is 5 + S, where S is the sum of dice 2 and 3. Before any trading, S averages 7, giving a fair value of 12.

- **Quote 1 (sell at 7):** An informed trader sells at 7 only if the sum is below 7. With die 1 = 5 the sum is at least 7, so this seller must have been noise. It tells us nothing.
- **Quote 2 (buy at 11.4):** An informed trader buys only if the sum is at least 12, which means S is at least 7 (probability 21/36). I put the public fair value before that quote at roughly 10.3. A noise trader would then buy at 11.4 with probability about 0.4.
- **Updating on the buy:** Weighting each S by the chance of seeing that buy, using these rough inputs, gives expected S ≈ 7.7. So the fair value is about 12.7.

**Setting the spread.** S has a standard deviation of about 2.4, so I quote roughly 2 points either side of 12.7. An informed trader would buy at 14.5 only if S is 10 or more, which has probability 6/36.

{"bid": 10.9, "ask": 14.5}

The public fair value is about **12.0**.

- **Starting point:** die 1 = 5, and the two unrevealed dice average 7, so the prior value is 12.
- **Quote 3 (sold at 10.9):** an informed trader sells there only if the sum is 10 or less. So this sale shifts weight toward low values.
- **Quote 2 (bought at 11.4):** an informed trader buys there only if the sum is 12 or more. So this buy shifts weight toward high values.
- **Quote 1 (sold at 7):** an informed trader would sell only if the sum were below 7. With die 1 = 5 that cannot happen, so this trade tells us nothing.
- **Combined estimate:** the two informative trades roughly cancel. The expected value of dice 2 + 3 comes out near 7.06, which puts fair value around 12.06.

I'm long 1, so I skew the quotes slightly lower to make selling a bit more likely than buying. The spread is fairly wide because the value still has a standard deviation of about 2.4 and informed traders arrive 35% of the time.

{"bid": 10.6, "ask": 13.2}

I'm quoting a bid of 9.2 and an ask of 15.8. Both are outside the range of possible settlement values, so an informed trader never trades against me.

- **Fair value:** Dice 1 and 2 sum to 9, and die 3 is uniform from 1 to 6. The contract therefore settles somewhere from 10 to 15, with an expected value of 12.5. The stage-2 trades went one each way, so they tell me little about die 3, and I'm using 12.5.
- **Informed traders (35%):** At my ask, a buyer's expected loss to me falls as the ask rises. At 13.1 that loss outweighs the noise profit. At 15 or above an informed buyer never trades, because the value can't exceed 15. The bid works the same way on the low side.
- **Noise traders (65%):** With no informed losses, I just want the spread that earns most from noise traders. The expected profit per side is about 0.65 × spread × P(noise exceeds spread). That is roughly flat and highest for a spread of about 3 to 3.5. So I set each side 3.3 from 12.5.
- **Position:** I'm flat, so I don't need to skew the quotes.

{"bid": 9.2, "ask": 15.8}

The settlement value is 9 plus die 3. Die 1 (5) and die 2 (4) are already revealed. So it settles somewhere from 10 to 15, and fair value is 12.5.

**Ask side.** Expected profit at ask *a* is the gain from noise traders minus the loss to informed traders. Noise traders buy when their valuation, Normal(12.5, 4.4), is above *a*, and each such trade earns *a* − 12.5. Informed traders buy only when the true value *v* is above *a*, and each such trade loses *v* − *a*.

| Ask | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14.0 | 0.358 | 0.058 | 0.30 |
| 15.0 | 0.463 | 0 | 0.46 |
| 15.5 | 0.483 | 0 | 0.48 |
| 16.0 | 0.485 | 0 | 0.49 |
| 16.5 | 0.473 | 0 | 0.47 |

At 15 and above the informed loss is zero, because the value can't exceed 15. Above that, profit only depends on the noise traders. Net profit peaks at about 15.8–16.0.

**Bid side.** The setup is symmetric around 12.5, so the best bid is about 9.2.

My position is flat, so there is no reason to skew either side.

{"bid": 9.2, "ask": 15.8}

game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
With nothing revealed yet, the expected sum of three fair dice is 10.5, and the standard deviation of the sum is about 2.96.

I chose the quote half-width h by trading off two effects on each side of the book:

| Half-width h | Noise-trader profit (0.65·h·P(N>h)) | Informed loss (0.35·E[(V−ask)⁺]) | Net per side |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0.33 | 0.16 | 0.17 |
| 3 | 0.31 | 0.09 | **0.22** |
| 4 | 0.24 | 0.04 | 0.20 |

A half-width of about 3 gives the highest net, so I quote 7.5 bid and 13.5 ask.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

Fair value is 10.5, the expected sum of three dice. Last quote's lack of a trade barely changes that.

I chose the half-spread by trading off profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders, per side:

| Half-spread | Net expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 1.5 | ≈0.10 |
| 2.0 | ≈0.17 |
| 2.5 | ≈0.215 |
| 3.0 | ≈0.225 |
| 3.5 | ≈0.22 |

Net profit peaks at a half-spread of about 3.0, so I'll quote 10.5 ± 3.0 again.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

Fair value is 10.5, the expected sum of three dice. There have been no trades, so nothing has changed that.

To choose the half-spread h around 10.5, I compared expected profit from noise traders against expected loss to informed traders:

| Ask | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12.5 | ≈ 0.33 | ≈ 0.16 | ≈ 0.17 |
| 13.0 | ≈ 0.33 | ≈ 0.11 | ≈ 0.22 |
| 13.5 | ≈ 0.31 | ≈ 0.085 | ≈ 0.225 |
| 14.0 | ≈ 0.28 | ≈ 0.06 | ≈ 0.22 |

A half-spread of about 3 is close to optimal, so I'll keep the same quote. The bid side is symmetric.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

Die 1 is 1, so the settlement value is 1 plus the sum of dice 2 and 3. Before any trading, that would put fair value at 8.

The three no-trades at 7.5 / 13.5 carry some information. An informed trader would have sold to me if the value were 7 or less. That happens when dice 2 and 3 sum to 6 or less. Updating on three straight no-trades pushes the dice 2 + 3 sum toward 7 or more. That moves my estimate of fair value to roughly 9.2.

I'll centre near 9.2 with a fairly wide spread, because informed traders are common (35%).

{"bid": 7.3, "ask": 11.1}

Die 1 came up 1, so the settlement value is 1 plus the sum of two dice. That gives a range of 3 to 13 with a mean of 8. The last quote (7.3 / 11.1) got no trade, which nudges the public fair value slightly above 8.

**Choosing the ask.** I checked a few ask levels against the two counterparty types:
- **Noise traders:** I gain about 0.65 × P(valuation above ask) × (ask − 8).
- **Informed traders:** I lose about 0.35 × E[(value − ask)⁺].

| Ask | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 9.5 | 0.155 |
| 10.0 | 0.23 |
| 10.5 | 0.26 |
| 11.0 | 0.27 |

Profit is fairly flat between about 10.5 and 11, so I'll quote an ask near 10.9.

**Choosing the bid.** The bid mirrors this around a fair value of about 8.05, which puts it near 5.3.

{"bid": 5.3, "ask": 10.9}

Die 1 = 1 and the other two dice average 7, so the prior fair value is 8. Quotes 4 and 5 both drew no trade. That nudges the estimate toward middle values, since an informed trader would have hit an extreme. The posterior mean comes out around 8.4. I'll quote roughly ±2 around that to protect against informed flow.

{"bid": 6.4, "ask": 10.4}

With dice 1 and 2 known (1 + 6 = 7), the settlement is 7 plus die 3. That makes it uniform over 8 to 13, with a fair value of 10.5. The earlier quotes drew no trades, so the history tells us little.

**Informed traders (probability 0.35):** they only trade if the true value is strictly above my ask or strictly below my bid. An ask of 13.0 and a bid of 8.0 sit at the extremes of the possible range, so an informed trader never trades against me.

**Noise traders (probability 0.65):** for a quote h away from 10.5, the expected gain on each side is roughly P(N(0,3) > h) × h. This peaks near h = 2.5, at about 0.2023 × 2.5 ≈ 0.51 per side. A tighter spread starts losing to informed traders. A wider one gets fewer noise trades.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 13.0}

The settlement value is 7 (dice 1 and 2) plus die 3, so it lands on 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 or 13 with equal chance. The public fair value is 10.5. The no-trade at quote 7 (bid 8, ask 13) only rules out the two extreme outcomes symmetrically, so the fair value stays 10.5.

**Choosing the ask.** I weighed the edge earned from noise traders against losses to informed traders when the value is above the ask:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 11.5 | +0.12 |
| 12.1 | +0.26 |
| 12.9 | +0.33 |
| 13.0 | +0.33 |
| 13.5 | +0.31 |

At 13.0 an informed trader never buys, because the value can't exceed 13. A noise trader still buys about 20% of the time, at 2.5 above fair value. The ask profit peaks around 13.0.

**Choosing the bid.** The setup is symmetric about 10.5, so the best bid is 8.0.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 13.0}

The final quote is set to maximise expected profit against informed and noise traders.

**Fair value.** Die 1 = 1 and die 2 = 6 are known, and die 3 averages 3.5. So the fair value is 10.5, and settlement is equally likely to be any of 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 or 13.

**Ask.**
- At an ask of 13.0, an informed trader never buys, because the value cannot exceed 13.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(N(0,3) > 2.5) ≈ 0.20, and each such sale earns 2.5.
- Expected profit is 0.65 × 0.20 × 2.5 ≈ 0.33.
- Asking lower adds more noise sales, but informed buyers then hit the ask when the value is 13. At 12.5 the expected profit is about 0.30, and at 12.1 it is about 0.26.
- Asking higher loses too many noise trades: at 13.5 the expected profit is about 0.31.
- So 13.0 is close to the best ask.

**Bid.** The same reasoning applies in reverse, so the best bid is 8.0.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 13.0}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Before anything is revealed, the sum of three dice has an expected value of 10.5 and a standard deviation of about 2.96. The quote needs a half-spread wide enough that the edge earned from noise traders outweighs the losses to informed traders.

Per side, the expected profit at half-spread h is roughly h·(1−Φ(h/3)) − 1.05·φ(h/3), where Φ is the normal distribution function and φ is the normal density.
- At h = 2 the expected profit is about 0.17.
- At h = 3 it is about 0.22, which is the best of the three.
- At h = 3.5 it is about 0.21.

So I quote 3 either side of 10.5, a bid of 7.5 and an ask of 13.5.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

Fair value is still 10.5, the expected sum of three dice. The last quote at 7.5/13.5 got no trade, which tells us almost nothing. A half-spread of about 3 gives the best expected edge, roughly 0.22 per side. Tighter quotes lose more to informed traders, and wider ones lose too much noise flow. So I keep the same quote.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

A buy at 13.5 raises my estimate of the fair value from 10.5 to roughly 11.9, so I'm quoting about 9.8 / 14.0 around that.

- **Prior:** the sum of three dice has mean 10.5 and a standard deviation of about 2.96.
- **Quote 1 (no trade):** this tells me little and slightly lowers the chance the sum is at either extreme.
- **Quote 2 (they bought at 13.5):**
  - An informed trader buys only if the sum is 14 or more. That has probability 35/216 ≈ 0.16, and the average sum in that case is 15.
  - A noise trader buys with probability about 0.16 (the chance that 10.5 plus noise with standard deviation 3 exceeds 13.5).
  - So the chance of a buy is about 0.45 if the sum is 14 or more, and about 0.10 otherwise.
  - The updated estimate is a weighted average of 15 (sum 14 or more) and 9.6 (sum below 14). That gives about 12.1, and the no-trade at quote 1 pulls it down a little to about 11.9.
- **Quote:** I'm short 1 unit, so the bid is set slightly closer to fair value than the ask.

{"bid": 9.8, "ask": 14.0}

Die 1 = 4 and dice 2 and 3 average 7, so the unconditional value is 11. The trade history moves this up.

**Buy at 13.5 in quote 2.** A total of 14 or more needs dice 2+3 ≥ 10, which has probability 6/36.
- An informed counterparty buys exactly when the total is at least 14.
- A noise trader buys about 16% of the time.
- So high totals are roughly 4 times more likely to produce that buy than low ones.

**No trade at 9.8 / 14 in quote 3.** This is consistent with totals between 10 and 14. It slightly lowers the weight on very high and very low totals.

**Rough Bayesian estimate.** These two pieces of evidence give E[dice 2+3] of about 8.4. That puts the fair value at about 12.4.

**Quote.** Allowing for some model uncertainty, I centre near 12.2–12.3. I quote fairly wide to guard against informed traders, and lean slightly up because I'm short 1.

{"bid": 10.8, "ask": 13.8}

Die 1 is 4, so the other two dice sum to 7 on average. That gives an unconditional value of 11.

The trading history pushes fair value higher. The buy at 13.5 in stage 1 is meaningfully more likely if the true sum is high. The no-trades at 7.5–13.5, 9.8–14 and 10.8–13.8 fit sums in the middle of the range. I weighted each possible two-dice sum by these four quotes, mixing 35% informed and 65% noise counterparties. That gives an expected two-dice sum of about 7.9, so fair value is about 11.9.

I quote roughly ±1.5 around that to cover the informed traders. I'm short 1 unit, so I nudge the bid up slightly to make buying a bit more likely.

{"bid": 10.5, "ask": 13.4}

Estimated fair value is about 12.8.

- **Prior:** with die 1 = 4, the expected sum is 4 + 7 = 11.
- **Update from the trades:** someone bought at 13.4 this stage and at 13.5 last stage. An informed buyer at those prices means a sum of at least 14, so the estimate moves up. The quotes with no trade (especially 10.8 / 13.8) partly offset this.
- **Posterior:** I weighted each possible sum by how likely the observed history would be under it, mixing 35% informed and 65% noise traders. That gives an expected sum of about 12.8.
- **Position:** I am short 2, so I set the quote slightly above fair value to make buying back a little more likely. The spread is about ±1.5 around 12.8 to guard against informed traders.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 14.4}

Die 1 and die 2 are both 4, so they sum to 8. The settlement value is therefore 8 plus die 3, which is equally likely to be any of 9 to 14. Its expected value is 11.5.

**How each price is scored:**
- An informed counterparty costs money only when the true value is beyond my quote. At an ask of 14.0 or above, it can never buy at a loss to me, because 14 is the maximum value.
- A noise trader values the contract at 11.5 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 3. At an ask of 11.5 + d, it buys with probability P(noise > d). Each such trade earns me d, and noise traders arrive with probability 0.65.

**Expected profit on the ask side for a few prices:**

| Ask | Cost from informed traders | Gain from noise traders | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12.9 | 0.07 | 0.29 | 0.22 |
| 13.5 | 0.03 | 0.33 | 0.30 |
| 14.0 | 0 | 0.33 | 0.33 |
| 14.5 | 0 | 0.31 | 0.31 |

An ask of 14.0 gives the highest expected profit.

**Bid side:** the same calculation mirrored around 11.5 gives a bid of 9.0. At 9.0 an informed trader can never sell to me at a loss, because 9 is the minimum value.

**Position:** I am only 1 unit short, which is well within the ±5 limit. Skewing the quotes to reduce it isn't worth giving up the better prices.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 14.0}

**Quote 8: bid 9.0, ask 14.0**

- **Settlement range:** The two revealed dice sum to 8, so the contract settles at 8 + die 3. That means it can only be 9 to 14, with a fair value of 11.5.
- **Quote 7 trade:** The counterparty sold to me at 9. An informed trader would only do that if the value were below 9, which is impossible. So it was a noise trader, and the fair value stays at about 11.5.
- **Why these prices:** Quoting at the edges of the range (bid 9, ask 14) means an informed trader can never profitably trade against me. Each side still earns about 2.5 from noise traders, whose valuations spread around 11.5 with standard deviation 3.
- **Comparison:**

| Ask | Expected profit on that side |
|---|---|
| 13.0 | about 0.24 |
| 13.5 | about 0.30 |
| 14.0 | about 0.33 |
| 14.5 | about 0.31 |

  14.0 is the best, and 9.0 is the matching best bid.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 14.0}

This is the last quote, and the position is flat (0), so I'll post a symmetric quote of bid 9.0 and ask 14.0.

**Fair value.** Dice 1 and 2 are both 4, so the contract settles at 8 + die 3. That means it settles somewhere from 9 to 14, with fair value 11.5.

**Trade history.** The sale at 9 on quote 7 must have come from a noise trader. An informed trader would only sell below 9, and the value can't be below 9. Quote 8 had no trade, but an informed trader wouldn't have traded against 9/14 anyway, so that tells me nothing. Fair value stays at 11.5.

**Choosing the ask.** Expected profit for each candidate ask:
- **Ask 13.5:** the noise-trader edge is about 0.33. An informed trader would buy if die 3 is 6, costing about 0.03, so the net is about 0.30.
- **Ask 14.0:** the noise-trader edge is about 0.33. An informed trader never buys, because the value can't be above 14, so the net is about 0.33.
- **Ask 14.5:** the net is about 0.31.

14.0 is the best of these.

**Choosing the bid.** The bid works the same way in reverse. At 9.0 an informed trader never sells, because the value can't be below 9, so the bid only fills against noise traders.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 14.0}

info.raw:
Fair value for the sum of three cards is about 27.2, and the main risk is the informed half of counterparties, so I'm quoting a wide spread around that.

**Fair value.** The deck holds 4×2, 3×10, 4×13 and 2×14, so the cards total 118 across 13 cards. The mean card is 118/13 ≈ 9.08. Expected sum of three cards ≈ 27.2.

**Uncertainty.**
- The variance of a single card is about 24.1.
- For three cards drawn without replacement, the variance is 3 × 24.1 × (10/12) ≈ 60.
- That gives a standard deviation of about 7.8.

**Spread.** Half of counterparties know the exact settlement and will only trade when it hurts me. The other half are noise traders whose valuations spread about 5.8 around fair value. To protect against the informed traders while still catching some noise flow, I'll quote roughly ±5.5 around fair value.

{"bid": 21.7, "ask": 32.8}

The public fair value has moved up to about 33.2 after the first buyer, so I'm centring around 34 and quoting wide.

- **Prior fair value:** the average card is 118/13 ≈ 9.08, so the sum of three cards has an expected value of about 27.2.
- **Which sums beat 32.8:** a sum above 32.8 needs no 2s among the dealt cards, and must not be 10+10+10.
  - The chance of that is 83/286 ≈ 0.29.
  - When it happens, the average sum is about 36.75.
  - In every other case, the average sum is about 23.3.
- **What the buy at 32.8 tells me:**
  - An informed counterparty buys only when the sum beats 32.8.
  - A noise trader valued around 27.2, with standard deviation 5.8, buys about 17% of the time.
  - Weighing these, the chance the sum is high rises to about 0.74.
  - The new public fair value is about 0.74 × 36.75 + 0.26 × 23.3 ≈ 33.2.
- **Why the quote is wide and tilted up:**
  - The possible sums are clustered in two groups rather than spread evenly, and informed traders make up half the flow. A wide spread limits what they can take from me.
  - I'm already short one unit, so I set the quote centre near 34, slightly above fair. That makes buying back a little more likely than selling again.

{"bid": 29.5, "ask": 38.5}

The quote is bid 38.0, ask 41.1.

**Prior after the reveal.** With card 1 = 14 known, the two hidden cards come from 4×2, 3×10, 4×13 and 1×14. Their expected sum is 17.3, so the plain expected total is about 31.3. The possible totals and their counts out of 66 equally likely pairs are:

| Total | 18 | 26 | 29 | 30 | 34 | 37 | 38 | 40 | 41 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Count (of 66) | 6 | 12 | 16 | 4 | 3 | 12 | 3 | 6 | 4 |

**Update on the history.** In stage 1 the counterparties bought at 32.8 and then at 38.5. Noise traders rarely buy that far above fair value, so two buys point strongly to informed buyers. Weighting each total by how likely those two buys were under it gives a posterior of about 87% on 40 or 41. The posterior mean is about 39.6.

**My quote.**
- **Ask 41.1:** this sits above the highest possible total, 41, so an informed buyer never takes it. Noise traders will sometimes buy there, which is profitable.
- **Bid 38.0:** I'm short 2 and the value is probably 40–41, so buying back below fair is good. The occasional loss to an informed seller (value 37 or lower) is smaller than the gain from noise sellers.

{"bid": 38.0, "ask": 41.1}

The revealed 14 and the trading history put the settlement value at about 40.2, most likely 40 or 41. I'm quoting 39.8 / 41.1 so informed traders have no reason to trade unless the low-probability cases are true.

**Prior after card 1 = 14.** The remaining 12 cards are four 2s, three 10s, four 13s and one 14. That gives 66 equally likely pairs for cards 2 and 3:

| Total S | Number of pairs |
|---|---|
| 18 | 6 |
| 26 | 12 |
| 29 | 16 |
| 30 | 4 |
| 34 | 3 |
| 37 | 12 |
| 38 | 3 |
| 40 | 6 |
| 41 | 4 |

The expected value from the cards alone is about 31.3.

- **Quote 1, buy at 32.8:** this favours S > 32.8, with likelihood about 0.58 against 0.08.
- **Quote 2, buy at 38.5:** this favours S > 38.5, with likelihood about 0.55 against 0.05.

**Quote.** A bid at 39.8 and an ask at 41.1 sit around that value.

{"bid": 39.8, "ask": 41.1}

The contract will most likely settle at 40 or 41, so I'll quote 39.6 / 41.1.

**What can settle.** The two revealed cards sum to 27 (14 + 13). Card 3 comes from the 11 cards left:

| Card 3 | Count | Probability | Settlement |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 4 | 4/11 | 29 |
| 10 | 3 | 3/11 | 37 |
| 13 | 3 | 3/11 | 40 |
| 14 | 1 | 1/11 | 41 |

- 29 with probability 4/11

- 40 with probability 3/11
- 41 with probability 1/11

The fair value is 388/11 ≈ 35.27.

**Ask.** If the ask is 41.0 or higher, an informed trader never buys, because the settlement can't exceed 41. A noise trader buys with probability about 16%, and I gain about 5.7 when that happens. That gives an expected profit of about 0.46. Lowering the ask to around 40 picks up more noise buyers, but I would sometimes lose to informed traders when the value is 41. That gives an expected profit of about 0.44. Raising the bid above 29 brings in informed sellers whenever the value is 29, which happens 4/11 of the time. game.description: A custom deck of 10 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 0, 1 card worth 4, 3 cards worth 5, 1 card worth 7, 2 cards worth 11, 2 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
The settlement value is the sum of 3 cards drawn without replacement.

**Fair value and uncertainty**
- The deck values add up to 78, so the average card is worth 7.8.
- The expected sum of 3 cards is 3 × 7.8 = **23.4**.
- The variance of a single card is 83.2 − 60.84 = 22.36.
- For 3 cards without replacement, the variance is 3 × 22.36 × 7/9 ≈ 52.2. The standard deviation is about **7.2**.

**Choosing the spread**
- Half of the counterparties are informed and know the value exactly. Their spread is about 7.2, compared with 5.4 for noise traders. So adverse selection is the main risk.
- **At a half-spread of 5:** noise traders earn me about 0.89 per side, but informed traders cost me about 1.05. That loses money.
- **At a half-spread of 8:** noise traders earn me about 0.56, and informed traders cost me about 0.48. That is a small profit.
- **At a half-spread of 10:** I earn about 0.32 and lose about 0.27. That is still slightly positive but smaller.
- A half-spread of about 8 around 23.4 works best, so I quote 15.4 / 31.4.

{"bid": 15.4, "ask": 31.4}

Fair value is about 23.4. The deck averages 7.8 per card, so three cards average 23.4, with a standard deviation of roughly 7.2.

The last quote (15.4 / 31.4) got no trade. That doesn't move fair value much, since the true sum very likely sits in that range anyway.

I'll tighten to about ±5 around fair value. That should catch more noise traders while still giving some protection against informed ones.

{"bid": 18.4, "ask": 28.4}

Fair value is about 16.4, so I'm quoting a bid of 12.5 and an ask of 20.5, shaded slightly lower because I'm long one unit.

**Prior after the reveal.** With card 1 = 5, nine cards remain: {0, 4, 5, 5, 7, 11, 11, 15, 15}. Their mean is 73/9 ≈ 8.11. That puts the expected sum of the two unseen cards at 16.2 and the expected total at about 21.2.

**Updating on the sale at 18.4.** At that point the public fair value was 23.4. An informed trader sells at 18.4 only if the total is below 18.4. That means the unseen two cards sum to 13 or less, which is true for 12 of the 36 possible pairs. Those 12 pairs average 8.8. The other 24 pairs average 19.9.
- A noise trader sells with probability P(N(23.4, 5.4) < 18.4) ≈ 0.18.
- If the pair is low, the chance of a sale is 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.18 ≈ 0.59.
- If the pair is high, it is 0.5 × 0.18 ≈ 0.09.
- The posterior weights are 12 × 0.59 ≈ 7.1 for low and 24 × 0.09 ≈ 2.1 for high.
- That gives a posterior mean for the two unseen cards of about 11.4.
- The fair value of the contract is therefore about 5 + 11.4 = 16.4.

**Spread.** The posterior is strongly two-peaked: totals near 13.8 or near 24.9. Informed traders will hit whichever side is wrong, so I'm keeping the spread wide.

{"bid": 12.5, "ask": 20.5}

The public fair value is about 16.7, so I'm quoting roughly 3.3 below it and 3.7 above it.

**Remaining cards.** With card 1 = 5, the 9 cards left are 0, 4, 5, 5, 7, 11, 11, 15, 15. On the deck alone, the expected sum is 5 + 2 × 8.11 ≈ 21.2.

**What the trading history tells us.** I weighted each possible total by how likely the past three quotes' outcomes were if that total were true:
- **Quote 1 (no trade at 15.4/31.4):** totals between 15.4 and 31.4 become more likely.
- **Quote 2 (they sold at 18.4):** totals below 18.4 become much more likely.
- **Quote 3 (no trade at 12.5/20.5):** totals between 12.5 and 20.5 become more likely.

**Updated estimate.** The expected total comes out at about **16.7**. The probability is spread as follows:
- about 58% on a total of 16 or 17;
- about 23% on 15 or less;
- about 19% on 20 or more.

**Quote choice.**
- **Bid 13.4:** an informed trader would only sell to me if the total is 12 or less, which is roughly 7% likely.
- **Ask 20.4:** an informed trader buys only if the total is 20 or more. The ask sits a bit wider on this side because those high totals average about 24, so losses there would be larger.
- **Noise traders:** they centre around 16.7 with standard deviation 5.4, so each side still has a reasonable chance of a profitable trade.
- **Position:** I'm only long 1, so I don't need to skew the quotes.

{"bid": 13.4, "ask": 20.4}

The third card is drawn from the 8 cards left after the 5 and the 0: 4, 5, 5, 7, 11, 11, 15, 15. The settlement value is 5 plus that card, so it is one of 9, 10, 10, 12, 16, 16, 20, 20, each with probability 1/8. Fair value is 113/8 ≈ 14.13.

**Ask.** I compared expected profit per quote across several asks:
- At 20.0, an informed trader never buys, because their valuation is at most 20 and they only buy above the ask.
- A noise trader buys about 14% of the time, for a gain of about 5.9 each time.
- Lower asks did worse. At 17 or 19, the informed buyers holding 16 or 20 cost more than the extra noise trades earn.

**Bid.** The same logic applies on the other side:
- At 9.0, an informed trader never sells, because their valuation is at least 9 and they only sell below the bid.
- A noise trader sells about 17% of the time, for a gain of about 5.1 each time.
- Bidding 10.1 earns slightly less, because informed sellers at 9 and 10 cost more than the extra noise trades earn.

My current long position of +1 doesn't change the expected-value calculation.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 20.0}

Only card 3 is still hidden, so I can calculate the settlement distribution exactly and pick the quote that maximises expected profit for this last trade.

**Settlement value**
- The cards left in the deck are 4, 5, 5, 7, 11, 11, 15 and 15. Card 3 is equally likely to be any of these eight.
- Cards 1 and 2 add up to 5.
- So settlement is 9, 10, 10, 12, 16, 16, 20 or 20, each with probability 1/8.
- The expected value is 5 + 73/8 = 14.125.

**Ask side**
- At an ask of 20.0, no informed trader buys, because the value is never above 20.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(z > 1.088), about 0.138, earning 5.875.
- Expected gain is 0.5 × 5.875 × 0.138 ≈ 0.405. This is the best ask I found:
  - An ask of 19 gives about 0.32, because informed traders buy when the value is 20.
  - An ask of 21 gives about 0.35, because noise traders rarely reach it.

**Bid side**
- At a bid of 9, no informed trader sells, because the value is never below 9.
- A noise trader sells with probability P(z < −0.949), about 0.171, earning 5.125.
- Expected gain is 0.5 × 5.125 × 0.171 ≈ 0.44. This is the best bid I found:
  - A bid of 10 gives about 0.40, because informed traders sell when the value is 9.
  - A bid of 8 gives about 0.39.

| 20 | both | 0.3125 |

An informed trader will buy from me when the value is 20 and sell to me when it is 0. Each of those trades costs me roughly 9 to 11 per unit. To cover that, I'm quoting a fairly wide spread centred on 11.25. That still leaves a decent chance of trading with noise traders, whose valuations spread around 11.25 with a standard deviation of 7.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 15.0}

With nothing revealed yet, the fair value is about **11.25**:

- Die 1 is at least 6 on faces 7 and 8, so the chance is 1/2.
- Die 2 is at least 6 on faces 10, 11, 12, 12 and 12, so the chance is 5/8.

The settlement can only be 0, 10 or 20:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.1875 |
| 10 | 0.50 |
| 20 | 0.3125 |

The lack of a trade at 7.5 / 15 shifts the estimate only slightly toward 10. An informed trader holding a value of 10 would not trade at those prices, so the fair value is now about **11.1**.

I can tighten the quotes a little and still expect a profit on each side:

- **Ask at 14.5.**
  - An informed buyer arrives when the value is 20, about 6% of the time, and costs 5.5.
  - A noise buyer arrives about 25% of the time and gains me about 3.4.
- **Bid at 8.**

{"bid": 8, "ask": 14.5}

Die 1 is 4, which is below 6, so it adds nothing to the settlement. The contract now depends only on die 2. Die 2 shows at least 6 on 5 of its 8 faces (10, 11, 12, 12, 12). So the contract settles at 10 with probability 5/8 and at 0 otherwise, and the fair value is 6.25.

**Ask:**
- If the ask is above 10, an informed buyer never trades with me. I then only face noise traders, whose valuation is 6.25 plus noise with standard deviation 7.
- Against noise alone, expected profit (ask − 6.25) × P(buy) peaks when the ask is about 0.75 standard deviations above fair. That is roughly 5.3 above, giving about 0.95 per quote.
- Pulling the ask below 10 adds more noise volume. But informed buyers then trade whenever the value is 10, and an ask at 10 only earns about 0.89. That is worse.
- So I quote the ask at about 11.5.

**Bid:**
- At a bid of 0, an informed seller never trades, since 0 is the lowest possible settlement value.
- Raising the bid above 0 adds about 0.04 of noise-trader profit per unit. It costs about 0.075 per unit from informed sellers when the value is 0. That is a net loss.

With die 1 revealed as 4, it cannot show 6 or more. Only die 2 matters. It shows 6 or more on 5 of its 8 faces (10, 11, 12, 12, 12), so the settlement is 10 with probability 5/8 and 0 otherwise. The fair value is 6.25.

The last trade was a buy at 11.5. An informed trader would never pay that, since the most the contract can settle at is 10. So the trade came from a noise trader, carries no information, and the fair value stays at 6.25.

game.title: Dice/cards count
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 1, 4, 7, 8.
- Die 2 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 3, 5, 10, 11, 12, 12, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of dice showing at least 6.

info.raw:
Fair value is 11.25. The chance that each die shows 6 or more is 1/2 for die 1 and 5/8 for die 2. So settlement is 0 with probability 0.1875, 10 with probability 0.5 and 20 with probability 0.3125.

I picked each side to balance profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders. Noise traders cross a quote that sits far from 11.25 less often, but each trade earns more. Informed traders only cross when the true value is beyond my quote.

**Ask side.** The informed trader buys only if the settlement value is 20.

| Ask | Expected net per quote |
|---|---|
| 14 | ≈ 0.39 |
| 15 | ≈ 0.58 |
| 16 | ≈ 0.69 |
| 17 | ≈ 0.76 |
| 18 | ≈ 0.78 |
| 19 | ≈ 0.77 |

**Bid side.** The informed trader sells only if the settlement value is 0.

| Bid | Expected net per quote |
|---|---|
| 8 | ≈ 0.53 |
| 6 | ≈ 0.73 |
| 5 | ≈ 0.74 |
| 4 | ≈ 0.72 |

The best choices are an ask of 18 and a bid of 5.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 18}

No new information has been revealed and there was no trade, so the public fair value stays at the prior expectation.

**Fair value**
- Die 1 shows at least 6 when it lands on 7 or 8: probability 2/4 = 0.5.
- Die 2 shows at least 6 when it lands on 10, 11, 12, 12 or 12: probability 5/8 = 0.625.
- The contract is worth 0, 10 or 20, with probabilities 0.1875, 0.5 and 0.3125.
- Expected value is 10 × (0.5 + 0.625) = 11.25.

**Ask**
- The informed trader buys only when the contract is worth 20, which happens with probability 0.3125.
- Noise traders buy when their valuation, 11.25 plus noise with standard deviation 7, is above the ask.
- Expected profit per quote is about 0.8 × (ask − 11.25) × P(noise > ask − 11.25), minus 0.2 × 0.3125 × (20 − ask).
- This is highest at about 0.78 for an ask 6 to 7 above fair value, so I set the ask at 18.

**Bid**
- With the bid below 10, the informed trader sells only when the contract is worth 0, which happens with probability 0.1875.
- The expected loss to the informed trader is then 0.2 × 0.1875 × bid.
- Profit is highest at about 0.74 for a bid around 6 below fair value, so I set the bid at about 5.2.

{"bid": 5.2, "ask": 18}

Die 1 shows 8, so it already counts. The contract settles at 10 plus 10 times whether die 2 is at least 6.

- Die 2 is at least 6 on 5 of its 8 faces (10, 11, 12, 12, 12), so the contract settles at 20 with probability 5/8 and at 10 with probability 3/8.
- Fair value is 0.625 × 20 + 0.375 × 10 = 16.25.

**Ask.** An informed trader knows the settlement value and only buys if it will be 20 and my ask is below 20. If I set the ask at 20 or above, I only trade with noise traders. Their valuations are centred at 16.25 with standard deviation 7. For the noise trade, the expected profit per quote is 0.8 × P(valuation above ask) × (ask − 16.25). That peaks at about ask = 21.5 to 21.7, giving roughly 0.95.

**Bid.** An informed trader only sells if the value will be 10 and my bid is above 10. A bid of exactly 10 avoids that loss entirely, because an informed trader valuing at 10 does not sell at 10. Noise-trader profit at a bid of 10 is about 0.8 × 0.186 × 6.25 ≈ 0.93. Raising the bid slightly earns a little more from noise traders but loses more to informed sellers. For example, a bid of 10.75 gives about 0.89.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 21.7}

The contract settles at 10 or 20, and it is worth about 22.5.

**Fair value.** Die 1 showed 8, which is at least 6, so it adds 10. Die 2 is at least 6 on 5 of its 8 faces (10, 11, 12, 12, 12). So settlement is 20 with probability 5/8 and 10 with probability 3/8. Expected value = 10 + 10 × 5/8 = 22.5.

The earlier no-trades don't change this. An informed trader would not have traded at my last quotes of 10 / 21.7 whatever the value. A noise trader's chance of not trading is the same either way. So the history tells me nothing new.

**Ask.** Any ask of at least 20 is never hit by an informed trader. Against noise traders, expected profit is roughly 0.8 × (a − 22.5) × P(noise > a − 22.5). This peaks at about 0.75 standard deviations above fair, which gives an ask of about 27.8.

**Bid.** A bid above 10 gets hit by an informed trader when the value is 10 (3/8 of the time). Expected profit for each bid:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 10 | 0.37 |
| 14 | 0.47 |
| 15 | 0.48 |
| 16 | 0.47 |
| 17.25 | 0.41 |

A bid of 15 gives the highest expected profit.

game.title: Dice/cards count
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12.
- Die 2 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/10), 4 (prob 1/5), 5 (prob 1/10), 6 (prob 1/10), 8 (prob 3/10), 9 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of dice showing at least 7.

info.raw:
The contract's expected value is 11.67, so I'm quoting a wide market around it: **bid 2.0, ask 20.0**.

**Settlement value distribution**
- Die 1 shows at least 7 with probability 4/6 = 2/3 (faces 7, 8, 10, 12).
- Die 2 shows at least 7 with probability 3/10 + 1/5 = 1/2 (faces 8 and 9).
- Value 0 needs neither die to count: (1/3)(1/2) = 1/6.
- Value 10 needs exactly one die to count: (2/3)(1/2) + (1/3)(1/2) = 1/2.
- Value 20 needs both dice to count: (2/3)(1/2) = 1/3.
- Expected value is 10 × (2/3 + 1/2) ≈ 11.67, which is the public fair value.

**Ask side**
An informed trader only buys at my ask when the true value is 20. Noise traders buy when their valuation, 11.67 plus noise with standard deviation 10, is above the ask.

| Ask | Expected gain from noise traders | Expected loss to informed traders | Net expected profit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18 | about 1.08 | 0.23 | about 0.85 |
| 20 | about 1.10 | 0 | about 1.10 |
| 22 | about 1.01 | 0 | about 1.01 |

The best ask is about 20, where the informed trader never buys.

**Bid side**
An informed trader sells to me only when the true value is 0. That costs me 0.35 × (1/6) × bid on average.

| Bid | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 1 | about 0.93 |
| 2 | about 0.93 |
| 3 | about 0.91 |
| 5 | about 0.80 |

The best bid is about 1 to 2, and I'm using 2.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 20.0}

**Fair value before any trades**

- Die 1 shows at least 7 (7, 8, 10 or 12) with probability 4/6 = 2/3.
- Die 2 shows at least 7 (8 or 9) with probability 3/10 + 1/5 = 1/2.
- So the settlement value is 0 with probability 1/6, 10 with probability 1/2, and 20 with probability 1/3.
- That gives an expected value of about 11.67.

**Updating on the sell at 2**

- An informed trader sells at 2 only if the value is 0.
- A noise trader sells if its valuation is below 2. With fair value 11.67 and noise standard deviation 10, that happens with probability about 0.167.
- Chance of a sell at 2 for each value:
  - If the value is 0: 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.167 ≈ 0.459.
  - If the value is 10 or 20: 0.65 × 0.167 ≈ 0.109.
- Updated probabilities: value 0 ≈ 0.458, value 10 ≈ 0.325, value 20 ≈ 0.217.
- The updated fair value is about 7.6.

**Choosing the quote**

Each figure below is my expected profit from that side of the quote.

- **Ask:**
  - Ask 15 earns about 0.72.
  - Ask 17 earns about 0.83.
  - Ask 19 earns about 0.87, the best.
  - Ask 20 earns about 0.87, with no loss to informed traders.
  - I choose 19.
- **Bid:**
  - A bid of 0 means an informed trader never sells to me, since the value is never below 0.
  - Noise traders still sell often enough to earn about 1.10.
  - That beats a bid of 1 (about 0.93) and a bid of 2 (about 0.73).

{"bid": 0, "ask": 19}

Die 2 = 5, which is below 7. So the contract pays 10 if die 1 is at least 7, and 0 otherwise. Before any trading, the chance that die 1 is at least 7 is 4/6.

**What the trades tell me**
- **Quote 1:** someone sold at my bid of 2.
  - If die 1 is low, the true value is 0 and an informed trader sells. The chance of a sale is 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.167 ≈ 0.46.
  - If die 1 is high, only a noise trader sells. The chance is 0.65 × 0.167 ≈ 0.11.
- **Quote 2:** no trade at 0 / 19. This was equally likely whether die 1 was high or low, so it tells me nothing.
- **Updated estimate:** P(die 1 high) = (4/6 × 0.1085) / (4/6 × 0.1085 + 2/6 × 0.4585) ≈ 0.32. Fair value is about 3.2.

**Choosing the ask**
- Asks between 8 and 10 lose money to informed buyers when the value is 10.
- At 10.1, informed traders never buy and noise buyers still bring about 1.1 of expected profit.

**Choosing the bid**
- At 0, informed sellers (who know the value is 0) do not trade.
- Noise sellers bring about 0.78 of expected profit.
- Bidding higher invites informed sellers and lowers expected profit.

Being long 1 also makes selling at a high ask welcome.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 10.1}

**Fair value.** Die 2 showed 5, which is below 7, so it adds nothing to settlement. The contract now settles at 10 if die 1 is at least 7, and 0 otherwise. Before any trading, the chance die 1 is at least 7 is 4/6 (faces 7, 8, 10, 12).

**What the trades tell us.**
- **Quote 1:** someone sold to me at 2.
  - If die 1 is below 7, the value is 0. An informed trader sells, and a noise trader sells about 16.7% of the time. Combined chance of a sale: about 0.46.
  - If die 1 is at least 7, the value is at least 10. Only a noise trader sells. Chance of a sale: about 0.11.
- **Quotes 2 and 3:** no trades. An informed trader would not have traded at those prices whatever the value, so these tell us nothing.
- **Result:** the chance die 1 is at least 7 falls to about 0.32. The public fair value is about 3.2.

**Ask.** Any ask at or above 10.1 is never hit by an informed trader. Against noise traders only, the best ask is about fair value + 7.5, which is about 10.7.

**Bid.** An informed trader values the contract at 0 or 10, so it never sells below 0. Against noise traders only, the best bid is about fair value − 7.5, which is about −4.3. The rules don't forbid a negative bid, but that is my assumption. I'll quote −4.2.

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 12 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 1, 4 cards worth 3, 3 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Bid 1.0, ask 8.9: a wide quote, because each trade has a 50% chance of being with someone who knows the settlement value.

**Distribution of the minimum.** Three cards are drawn from 12, so there are C(12,3) = 220 possible hands.

| Smallest card | Count | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 55 | 25% |
| 3 | 130 | 59% |
| 9 | 31 | 14% |
| 14 | 4 | 1.8% |

The fair value is 780/220 ≈ 3.55.

**Ask side.** An informed counterparty buys from me whenever the value is 9 or 14. With a fair value of 3.55, that loss is large.
- Noise buyers only make up for it at roughly 8.5 or higher.
- I quote 8.9, which mostly avoids losing money on this side.

**Bid side.** An informed counterparty sells to me only when the value is 1 (25% chance). At a bid of 1.0 or slightly above, that costs me almost nothing.
- About 18% of noise traders still sell to me there, each worth about 2.5 to me.
- That gives an expected gain of roughly 0.46 per noise arrival.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 8.9}

I'm quoting a bid of 1.1 and an ask of 9.0. The bid is well below fair value to stay clear of informed sellers, and the ask sits just at the 9 card value.

**Fair value.** I worked out the distribution of the smallest card from the 220 equally likely three-card hands:

| Smallest card | Hands | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 55 | 0.25 |
| 3 | 130 | 0.59 |
| 9 | 31 | 0.14 |
| 14 | 4 | 0.02 |

The expected settlement is 780 / 220 ≈ 3.55. The previous quote (1 / 8.9) drew no trade, which tells us almost nothing new.

**Bid.**
- Any bid above 1 gets sold into by informed traders whenever the card is 1, which is 25% of the time.
- Any bid above 3 also gets sold into whenever the card is 3. That is very costly, so the bid must stay at 3 or below.
- I compared bids by expected profit per quote:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 2.0 | about +0.10 |
| 1.5 | about +0.18 |
| 1.1 | about +0.22 (best) |

**Ask.**
- Any ask below 9 gets bought by informed traders whenever the card is 9 or 14. That loses about 5.6 per trade, which outweighs the profit from noise traders.
- At 9.0, informed traders only buy when the card is 14 (about 2% of the time). Noise traders still occasionally buy far above fair value, so the expected profit is small but positive.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 9.0}

Fair value is about 2.2, so I'll quote bid 1.0 and ask 4.8.

**Fair value from the cards.** Card 1 is 9, so 11 cards remain: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s. Two of them are dealt.
- P(min = 1) = 10/55
- P(min = 3) = 30/55
- P(min = 9) = 15/55
- Expected value from the cards alone: 235/55 ≈ 4.27

**Updating on the trade history.**
- **Quote 2 (sale at 1.1):** An informed trader only sells at 1.1 if the value is 1. A noise trader centred near 3.4 sells below 1.1 only about 21% of the time. So this sale strongly suggests the value is 1.
- **Quote 1 (no trade, bid 1 / ask 8.9):** An informed trader would have bought if the value were 9 or more. The lack of a trade makes a value of 9 less likely.
- **Posterior:** P(1) ≈ 0.62, P(3) ≈ 0.32, P(9) ≈ 0.07.
- **Fair value:** about 2.2.

**Bid.** At 1.0, an informed trader never sells, because a value of 1 is not below 1.0. A noise trader sells about 33% of the time, earning about 1.2 per trade.

**Ask.** Only a value of 9 makes an informed trader buy below 9, and that is about 7% likely. The ask needs to be high enough that noise buyers outweigh that loss. My estimates of expected profit for each ask:
- 3.5: about +0.02
- 4.5: about +0.08
- 5.5: about +0.08

The best is around 4.8.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 4.8}

Card 1 is a 9, so the settlement is the minimum of 9 and two cards drawn from the 11 left (one 1, four 3s, two 9s, four 14s).

**Prior from the cards**
- P(settle = 1) = 2/11
- P(settle = 3) = 6/11
- P(settle = 9) = 3/11
- Expected value ≈ 4.27

**Update on quote 3 (bid 1 / ask 4.8, no trade)**
- An informed trader would have bought at 4.8 if the value were 9. If the value were 1 or 3, it would not have traded.
- A noise trader would not have traded with probability ≈ 0.45.
- So the chance of seeing no trade is about 0.73 if the value is 1 or 3, but only about 0.23 if it is 9.
- Updated probabilities: 1 ≈ 0.22, 3 ≈ 0.67, 9 ≈ 0.10.
- Updated fair value ≈ 3.2.

**Ask:** I compared the profit from noise buyers against the loss to an informed buyer when the value is 9.
- An ask around 5–6 comes out slightly positive.
- I am already long one unit, so I lean slightly toward selling and set the ask at 5.8.

**Bid:** An informed trader only sells to me below 3 if the value is 1.
- A bid near 1 loses almost nothing to informed sellers.
- It still picks up noise sellers at about 2 below fair value.
- I set the bid at 1.1.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 5.8}

Card 2 is the 1, and the deck has only one card worth 1. So the minimum of the dealt cards is certainly **1**, and the settlement value is known to be exactly 1.

**Who trades with me**
- Informed traders value the contract at exactly 1. They won't trade if my bid is below 1 and my ask is above 1.
- Noise traders value it at 1 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.8. These are the only counterparties I can trade with.

**Choosing the spread**
- My expected profit on each side is the edge times the chance of a fill: edge × P(noise valuation beyond my quote).
- With noise of standard deviation 2.8, this is largest at an edge of about 0.75 × 2.8 ≈ 2.1.
- That gives an ask of 3.1 and a bid of -1.1, centred on the known value of 1.

**Position limits**
- I am long 2, so one more purchase would take me to the +3 limit. Both sides are allowed this quote.

{"bid": -1.1, "ask": 3.1}

The settlement value is already fixed. Card 2 is the deck's only 1, and no card is lower, so the minimum is 1.

- **Informed traders** know the value is 1, so they will never buy at any ask above 1.
- **Noise traders** value the contract at 1 + N(0, 2.8²). If I post an ask a, they buy with probability P(noise > a − 1), and my profit per sale is a − 1.
- Write x = (a − 1)/2.8. Then I want to maximise x·(1 − Φ(x)), where Φ is the standard normal distribution function. That peaks at x ≈ 0.75, which gives a ≈ 1 + 2.1 = 3.1.

So I post ask 3.1 and no bid, since my bid is pulled.

{"bid": null, "ask": 3.1}

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 2, 4, 8, 8.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/5), 2 (prob 1/5), 6 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/10), 12 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 9.09, and I'm quoting around it with a spread of about ±1.2. That spread protects against informed traders, since the possible settlement values sit far apart (4 to 12). It is still narrow enough to trade profitably with noise traders.

**Highest of die 1 and die 2**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 4 | 0.125 |
| 6 | 0.125 |
| 7 | 0.125 |
| 8 | 0.375 |
| 12 | 0.25 |

The expected value of this two-die maximum is 8.125.

**Adding die 3**

| Die 3 | Probability | Expected settlement |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 1 or 2 | 0.6 | 8.125 (die 3 never matters) |
| 6 | 0.1 | 8.375 (a 4 is lifted to 6) |
| 9 | 0.1 | 0.75 × 9 + 0.25 × 12 = 9.75 |
| 12 | 0.2 | 12 |

Fair value = 0.6 × 8.125 + 0.1 × 8.375 + 0.1 × 9.75 + 0.2 × 12 = **9.0875**.

{"bid": 7.9, "ask": 10.3}

Expected value of the max is about **9.09**:

- **Max of dice 1 and 2:**
  - 4 with probability 2/16.
  - 6 with probability 2/16.
  - 7 with probability 2/16.
  - 8 with probability 6/16.
  - 12 with probability 4/16.
  - Its expected value is 8.125.
- **Die 3 shows 0, 1 or 2 (probability 0.6):** the max is the max of dice 1 and 2, worth 8.125.
- **Die 3 shows 6 (probability 0.1):** the max is worth 8.375.
- **Die 3 shows 9 (probability 0.1):** the max is worth 9.75.
- **Die 3 shows 12 (probability 0.2):** the max is 12.

Combined: 0.6 × 8.125 + 0.1 × 8.375 + 0.1 × 9.75 + 0.2 × 12 ≈ **9.09**.

There was no trade on the first quote, so there is little new information. I'll keep the quote centred near 9.1 and tighten it slightly to 8.0 / 10.2.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 10.2}

Fair value is about 8.1. I'm quoting bid 6.9 / ask 9.1, set a little low because I'm long one unit.

**Fair value.** Die 3 = 1 no longer matters. Die 1 is at least 2 and die 2 is at least 4, so the maximum is always at least 4. The settlement is therefore max(die 1, die 2), with each of the 16 combinations equally likely:

| Die 1 | Maxima over die 2 faces (4, 6, 7, 12) | Sum |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 4, 6, 7, 12 | 29 |
| 4 | 4, 6, 7, 12 | 29 |
| 8 (two faces) | 8, 8, 8, 12 | 36 each |

The expected value is 130/16 ≈ 8.125. The possible settlement values are:
- 4 with probability 2/16
- 6 with probability 2/16
- 7 with probability 2/16
- 8 with probability 6/16
- 12 with probability 4/16

**Adverse selection.**
- An informed trader with a value of 12 will buy at any ask below 12.
- An informed trader with a value of 4 or 6 will sell at a bid of 6.9.
- With a value of 7, they would sell only if my bid were above 7.

So I quote roughly ±1.1 around fair.

**Inventory.** I'm long one unit, so I shade both prices slightly lower.

{"bid": 6.9, "ask": 9.1}

Die 3 rolled a 1, so it can never be the maximum. The contract now settles at the larger of die 1 and die 2.

**Prior expected value**
- If die 1 is 2 or 4, the maximum is just die 2: the values are 4, 6, 7 or 12, with mean 7.25.
- If die 1 is 8, the maximum is 8, 8, 8 or 12, with mean 9.
- Each case has probability 1/2, so the expected value is (7.25 + 9) / 2 = 8.125.

**Updating on the buy at 9.1**
- The only settlement value above 9.1 is 12, which happens when die 2 shows 12. Its prior probability is 1/4.
- A noise trader buys at 9.1 with probability P(Z > 0.375) ≈ 0.354, where Z is a standard Normal.
- If the value is 12, a buy happens with probability 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.354 ≈ 0.483. Otherwise it happens with probability 0.8 × 0.354 ≈ 0.283.
- The updated probability of 12 is (0.25 × 0.483) / (0.25 × 0.483 + 0.75 × 0.283) ≈ 0.36.
- If die 2 is not 12, the expected value is (5.67 + 8) / 2 ≈ 6.83.
- The updated fair value is 0.36 × 12 + 0.64 × 6.83 ≈ 8.7.

**Quote**
- The settlement values are lumpy: 4, 6, 7, 8 or 12.
- An informed trader would sell to me below about 7 and buy from me above 10.
- So I set a fairly wide spread around 8.7, with the bid near 7 and the ask near 10, to limit losses to informed traders.

{"bid": 7.1, "ask": 10.1}

The settlement is the larger of die 1 (revealed as 8) and die 2. Die 3 (revealed as 1) can't matter, since it is below 8.

**Settlement value**

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 2, 4, 8, 8.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/5), 2 (prob 1/5), 6 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/10), 12 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
Expected value of the max is about 9.09: P(max ≥ 12) = 0.4, and the remaining mass sits mostly at 8 and 9. I quote roughly ±1 around that, to balance the risk from informed traders against the flow from noise traders.

{"bid": 8.1, "ask": 10.1}

Expected settlement value before anything is revealed is about 8.98, so I'm keeping my quote centred near 9.

**Max of dice 1 and 2.** Pairing die 1 with die 2 gives this distribution:

| Max of dice 1 and 2 | 4 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 2/16 | 2/16 | 2/16 | 6/16 | 4/16 |

Its expected value is 130/16 = 8.125.

**Bringing in die 3:**
- Die 3 shows 0, 1 or 2 (probability 0.6): the maximum is unchanged, with expected value 8.125.
- Die 3 shows 6 (probability 0.1): the maximum is at least 6, with expected value 134/16 = 8.375.
- Die 3 shows 9 (probability 0.1): the maximum is at least 9, with expected value 138/16 = 8.625.
- Die 3 shows 12 (probability 0.2): the maximum is 12.

**Overall expected value:** 0.6 × 8.125 + 0.1 × 8.375 + 0.1 × 8.625 + 0.2 × 12 ≈ **8.98**.

**Quote.** The first quote (8.1 / 10.1) got no trade, which tells me little. I'll post a spread of about 2, centred at 9, against noise with standard deviation 2.6.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 10.0}

Die 3 = 6, so the contract settles at the largest of die 1, die 2 and 6. That leaves 16 equally likely combinations:

- **Die 1 = 2 or 4** (each combination): settlement is 6, 6, 7, 12 across the four faces of die 2.
- **Die 1 = 8** (two faces): settlement is 8, 8, 8, 12.

So the expected value is (31 + 31 + 36 + 36) / 16 = **8.375**.

The settlement distribution is: 6 with probability 4/16, 7 with 2/16, 8 with 6/16, and 12 with 4/16.

I am quoting about 1 point either side of 8.375, since noise traders' valuations spread by 2.6 around that.

- **Ask at 9.4:** an informed counterparty buys only when the value is 12, about 2.6 against me.
- **Bid at 7.4:** an informed counterparty sells only when the value is 6 or 7, about 1 against me.

Noise trades on both sides should cover these losses.

{"bid": 7.4, "ask": 9.4}

Fair value is about 7.95 after the trade, so I quote 6.9 bid and 8.9 ask, a little below centre because I'm long.

**Prior fair value with die 3 = 6.** The settlement is the max of die 1, die 2 and 6. Across the 16 equally likely die 1 × die 2 combinations:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | 4/16 |
| 7 | 2/16 |
| 8 | 6/16 |
| 12 | 4/16 |

The mean is 134/16 = 8.375.

**Update for the sale at 7.4.**
- An informed trader sells only if the value is below 7.4, which means 6 or 7.
- A noise trader sells with probability Φ((7.4 − 8.375)/2.6) ≈ 0.354.
- So the chance of a sale is 0.483 if the value is 6 or 7, and 0.283 if it is 8 or 12.

| Settlement | Posterior weight |
|---|---|
| 6 | 1.93 |
| 7 | 0.97 |
| 8 | 1.70 |
| 12 | 1.13 |

The posterior mean is about **7.95**.

**Quote choice.**
- I keep the spread around ±1 to protect against informed traders, who would buy only if the value is 12.
- A bid at 6.9 sits just below 7, so an informed seller only hits it if the value is 6.

{"bid": 6.9, "ask": 8.9}

Die 3 = 6 and die 1 = 8, so the contract settles at 8 unless die 2 shows 12. Each die 2 face has probability 1/4.
- Settlement is 8 with probability 0.75 and 12 with probability 0.25.
- Public fair value is 0.75 × 8 + 0.25 × 12 = 9.

**Ask side.**
- An informed trader who knows the value is 12 (probability 0.2 × 0.25 = 0.05) buys at any ask below 12. That loses me 12 − ask.
- An informed trader who knows the value is 8 won't buy at an ask above 8.
- A noise trader (probability 0.8) values the contract at 9 plus noise with standard deviation 2.6. It buys if that valuation is above my ask. Its noise tells me nothing about the true value, so each sale earns me ask − 9 on average.
- Weighing these, expected profit peaks at about +0.31 for an ask near 11.3 to 11.5.

**Bid side.**
- Any bid above 8 gets sold into by the informed trader who knows the value is 8. That loss outweighs the noise traders' value, giving only about +0.1.
- For bids at 8 or below, only noise traders sell to me. Expected profit peaks at about +0.35 for a bid near 7.0.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.4}

Die 1 = 8 and die 3 = 6, so the contract settles at max(8, die 2).

**Settlement value**
- Die 2 rolls 4, 6 or 7 with probability 3/4, giving a settlement of 8.
- Die 2 rolls 12 with probability 1/4, giving a settlement of 12.
- The prior fair value is 0.75 × 8 + 0.25 × 12 = 9.

**Update from quote 5 (7 / 11.4, no trade)**
- An informed trader who knew the value was 12 would have bought at 11.4, so no trade counts slightly against 12.
- I'm assuming a noise trader's valuation centres on the then-public fair value of 9. A valuation landing between 7 and 11.4 then has probability about 0.60.
- If the value is 8, the chance of no trade is 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.60 ≈ 0.68.
- If the value is 12, the chance of no trade is 0.8 × 0.60 ≈ 0.48.
- The updated probability of 12 is 0.25 × 0.48 / (0.25 × 0.48 + 0.75 × 0.68) ≈ 0.19.
- The fair value is now about 8.76.

**Bid**
- If the bid is 8 or lower, an informed seller never trades with me, because the value is at least 8.
- Weighing the chance a noise trader sells against my edge on each trade, the expected profit is highest with a bid around 6.8 (about 0.35).

**Ask**
- Any ask below 12 loses to an informed buyer when the value is 12.
- Balancing that loss against what I earn from noise buyers, an ask around 11.0–11.2 gives the highest expected profit (about 0.31).

info.raw:
I priced the quote on the expected minimum of the three dealt cards, then set each side where noise-trader profit outweighs losses to informed traders.

**Distribution of the minimum.** There are C(12,3) = 220 equally likely hands.

| Minimum | Count | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 220 − C(11,3) = 55 | 25.0% |
| 3 | C(11,3) − C(7,3) = 130 | 59.1% |

- If the bid is above 3, informed traders sell whenever the value is 1 or 3, which is about 84% of the time. That is too costly.
- At a bid of exactly 1.0, informed traders never sell, because no value is strictly below 1.
- Noise traders still sell about 18% of the time. Each such trade earns about 2.55, so the expected profit is roughly +0.23 per quote.

**Ask side.**
- An ask anywhere between 3 and about 8 loses money, because informed buyers holding a 9 or 14 cost more than noise buyers pay.
- At an ask of 9.0, informed traders buy only when the value is 14, which is 1.8% of the time.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

| Minimum | Count | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 55 | 0.25 |
| 3 | 130 | 0.59 |
| 9 | 31 | 0.14 |
| 14 | 4 | 0.018 |

- At 1, no informed trader sells to me, because a true value of 1 is not below my bid. Noise traders sell about 19% of the time for about 2.5 profit, so the edge is about +0.23.
- At 2, informed traders holding a true value of 1 sell to me and cost about 0.125. That pushes the net slightly below the bid at 1.

**Ask.**
- Quoting inside 9 lets informed traders buy whenever the true value is 9 or 14. At an ask of 6 the net edge is about −0.05, and at 8 it is about break-even.
- At 9, only a true value of 14 hurts me, and the net edge is about +0.02.

**Settlement distribution.** Card 1 is 9, so the settlement is min(9, c2, c3). The other two cards come from the 11 left: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s.

- P(min = 3) = (45/55) × (1 − C(6,2)/C(10,2)) = (45/55) × (30/45) = 30/55 ≈ 0.55
- P(min = 9) = 15/55 ≈ 0.27

|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | 0.27 | 0.225 | about −0.05 |
| 8 | 0.136 | 0.17 | about +0.03 |
| 9 | 0 | 0.107 | about +0.11 |

An ask of 9 is best: it removes the informed loss and still earns about 0.11 from noise buyers.

**Bid side.** Informed traders sell into my bid only when the value is 1 (18% of the time they arrive), and the loss is bid − 1.

| Bid | Expected informed loss | Expected noise gain | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0 | 0.091 | 0.237 | about +0.15 |
| 1.5 | 0.045 | 0.223 | about +0.18 |
| 1.2 | 0.018 | 0.209 | about +0.19 |

A bid of 1.2 gives the highest expected profit, about +0.19.

{"bid": 1.2, "ask": 9.0}

I'd quote **bid 1.8, ask 9.0**: the ask sits right at the top possible value, and the bid is set to catch noise sellers while risking little against an informed seller.

**Fair value**

The 11 cards left are: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s. Two more cards are dealt from them, and settlement is the smallest of 9 and those two cards.

- Settles at 1 if a 1 is dealt: 10/55.

**Ask**

**Bid**

info.raw:

- At 3, about 0.79.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 13.0}

- A noise trader sells there with probability Φ(−0.82), about 0.21.

Updated probabilities for the minimum:

| Minimum | Probability |
|---|---|
| 2 | 0.42 |
| 9 | 0.30 |
| 13 | 0.27 |

The updated fair value is about 7.1.

- **Bid:** an informed trader sells whenever the minimum is below my bid, which is about 42% likely for any bid above 2. Expected profit peaks with a bid of about 2.5.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 12.5}

The settlement value is now known exactly. Card 1 is a 2, and that is the lowest card in the deck, so the minimum of the two dealt cards must be 2. That makes the public fair value exactly 2. An informed trader also values the contract at 2, so it will never trade with me at a bid below 2 or an ask above 2.

Noise traders value the contract at 2 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 6.3. Against them, each side of my quote earns x × P(noise > x), where x is the distance from 2. This is largest when x/σ ≈ 0.75, so x ≈ 4.7.

That gives a bid of 2 − 4.7 = −2.7 and an ask of 2 + 4.7 = 6.7. My position of +1 is far from the ±5 limits, so both sides can be quoted.

{"bid": -2.7, "ask": 6.7}

Card 1 is a 2, the lowest card in the deck, so the contract settles at exactly 2.

**Informed counterparty:** it values the contract at exactly 2. Any bid below 2 and ask above 2 means it never trades with me, so it costs me nothing.

**Noise trader:** its valuation is 2 + N(0, 6.3).
- If I set my spread d away from 2 on each side, my expected profit per side is d·Φ(−d/6.3).
- This is largest when z·φ(z) = Φ(−z), which gives z ≈ 0.75.
- So d ≈ 0.75 × 6.3 ≈ 4.7.

That gives a bid of 2 − 4.7 = −2.7 and an ask of 2 + 4.7 = 6.7. My position of +1 allows trading on either side.

game.description: A custom deck of 22 cards is shuffled: 2 cards worth 2, 3 cards worth 3, 4 cards worth 4, 4 cards worth 5, 2 cards worth 12, 4 cards worth 13, 3 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Fair value is the expected minimum of 3 cards drawn from 22, which comes to about **3.77**.

**Distribution of the minimum** (out of C(22,3) = 1540 hands):

| Min | Probability |
|---|---|
| 2 | 0.260 |
| 3 | 0.299 |
| 4 | 0.256 |
| 5 | 0.131 |
| 12 or more | 0.055 |

**Choosing the quote:**
- The minimum is usually 2 to 5, but there is a small chance it is 12 or more. An informed buyer in that case would cost me a lot, so I keep the ask a bit wide.
- On the bid side, an informed seller holding a 2 is fairly likely (26%). A bid a little below 3 limits that loss.
- Noise traders have a standard deviation of 2.3, so a spread of about ±1 around fair value still captures a reasonable amount of their flow.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 4.9}

The contract settles at the smallest of the 3 dealt cards. I estimate its fair value at about **3.77**, so I'll quote **2.8 / 4.8**.

**How I got the fair value**

There are C(22,3) = 1540 ways to deal 3 cards. For each card value k, the chance that the minimum is at least k is C(number of cards ≥ k, 3) / 1540. The expected minimum is 2 plus each of these probabilities weighted by the gap to the next card value:

| Minimum at least | Cards that qualify | Probability | × gap to next value | Adds |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 20 | 1140/1540 = 0.740 | × 1 | 0.740 |
| 4 | 17 | 680/1540 = 0.442 | × 1 | 0.442 |
| 5 | 13 | 286/1540 = 0.186 | × 1 | 0.186 |
| 12 | 9 | 84/1540 = 0.055 | × 7 | 0.382 |
| 13 | 7 | 35/1540 = 0.023 | × 1 | 0.023 |
| 15 | 3 | 1/1540 = 0.001 | × 2 | 0.001 |

E[min] ≈ 2 + 0.740 + 0.442 + 0.186 + 0.382 + 0.023 + 0.001 ≈ **3.77**.

**Quote**

Quote 1 at 2.7 / 4.9 traded nothing, so the fair value hasn't moved. The minimum is almost always between 2 and 5. An informed counterparty will often know the true value is near one end of that range, so I keep a fairly wide spread. I'm tightening it slightly around 3.77 to catch more noise-trader flow.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 4.8}

Fair value is about 3.2, so I quote a bid of 2.4 and an ask of 3.8, leaning slightly toward selling because I'm long.

**Value given card 1 = 4.** The settlement value is min(4, card 2, card 3). The other two cards come from the 21 left: two 2s, three 3s, three 4s, four 5s, two 12s, four 13s and three 15s.
- P(at least one 2) = 1 − (19/21 × 18/20) = 78/420 ≈ 0.186, giving a minimum of 2.
- P(no 2, at least one 3) = 342/420 − 240/420 = 102/420 ≈ 0.243, giving a minimum of 3.
- Otherwise (≈ 0.571) the minimum is 4.
- That gives an expected value of about 3.39.

**What the stage-1 trade tells us.** Someone sold to me at 2.8. Given card 1 = 4, an informed trader would only sell there if the value is 2. Updating on that sale:
- P(value = 2) rises to about 0.285.
- P(value = 3) is about 0.213 and P(value = 4) about 0.502.
- Fair value falls to roughly 3.2.

**Quote.**
- **Ask:** the value can't exceed 4, so an ask near 4 loses little to informed buyers. 3.8 captures noise buyers well above fair value and helps unwind my long.
- **Bid:** 2.4 sits about 0.8 below fair. That limits losses to informed sellers when the value is 2, while still catching noise sellers.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 3.8}

Fair value is about 3.39, so I'll bid 2.8 and offer 4.0. Since I'm long one, both quotes sit slightly toward selling.

1. **Value given card 1 = 4.** The settlement can only be 2, 3 or 4, because the minimum can't exceed 4. The other 21 cards are: two 2s, three 3s, three 4s, four 5s, two 12s, four 13s and three 15s. There are 210 possible pairs for cards 2 and 3.
   - Pairs with no 2: 171 of 210.
   - Pairs with no 2 and no 3: 120 of 210.
   - So P(min = 2) = 39/210, P(min = 3) = 51/210 and P(min = 4) = 120/210.
   - Expected value = (2×39 + 3×51 + 4×120) / 210 = 711/210 ≈ **3.39**.

2. **Ask at 4.0.** An informed trader whose card says 4 only buys if the ask is below 4, so this loses nothing to them. A noise trader still buys about 40% of the time, earning about 0.6 per trade over fair value.

3. **Bid at 2.8.** An informed trader whose card says 3 won't sell to me at this price. Only the case where the true value is 2 hurts me there. Noise traders sell often enough at about 0.6 below fair value to make the bid worthwhile.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 4.0}

Card 3 is drawn from the remaining 20 cards, and settlement is min(4, card 3):
- It is 2 with probability 2/20.
- It is 3 with probability 3/20.
- It is 4 with probability 15/20.

So the expected value from the cards alone is 3.65.

Both earlier fills were counterparties selling to me at 2.8. That is slightly more likely if an informed trader knew a 2 was coming. I nudge public fair value down to about 3.5.

I am long 2, so I skew my quotes lower to encourage a sale. An ask at 3.6 is only filled by informed traders when the value is 4, which costs me 0.4. Noise traders will often buy there, which cuts my long position.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 3.6}

Two 4s have been dealt, so 20 cards remain: 2×2, 3×3, 2×4, 4×5, 2×12, 4×13 and 3×15.

**Fair value.** The contract settles at min(4, card 3).
- Card 3 = 2 with probability 2/20.
- Card 3 = 3 with probability 3/20.
- Otherwise (15/20) the settlement is 4.

Expected settlement = (2·2 + 3·3 + 15·4)/20 = 3.65. The settlement can never exceed 4.

**Choosing the ask.**
- **Informed trader:** they only buy if the settlement is above my ask. Any ask of 4.0 or more means they never buy, so they cannot cost me anything.
- **Noise trader:** valuations are 3.65 plus Normal noise with SD 2.3. Expected profit per noise arrival is (ask − 3.65) × P(valuation > ask).
- **Best edge:** for a normal distribution, edge × P(valuation > ask) is largest when the edge is about 0.61 × SD, roughly 1.4. That puts the ask at about 5.1.
  - The chance a noise trader buys is then about 27%.
  - Expected profit is about 0.8 × 0.27 × 1.4 ≈ 0.30.
  - An ask of 4.0 would give only about 0.12.

I'm long 3, so a sale also cuts my exposure. My bid is pulled at +3, so it stays null.

game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 10.
- Die 2 (4 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/10), 3 (prob 3/10), 4 (prob 1/5), 5 (prob 2/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dice.

info.raw:
The expected settlement value before any reveal is about 2.18. I quote wide because informed traders gain a lot when the value is 0 or 5.

**Settlement distribution (minimum of the two dice)**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.325 |
| 2 | 0.225 |
| 3 | 0.225 |
| 4 | 0.075 |
| 5 | 0.15 |

The expected value is 0.3·2 + 0.2·2.375 + 0.4·2.75 = **2.175**.

**Choosing each side**

For each candidate price I weighed two things:
- **Gain from noise traders:** they arrive with probability 0.65 and value the contract at 2.175 plus noise with standard deviation 1.8.
- **Loss to informed traders:** they arrive with probability 0.35 and know the true value.

- **Ask:** expected profit per quote is about 0.04 at 3.0, 0.09 at 3.3, 0.12 at 3.6, 0.13 at 4.0 and 0.13 at 4.3. It peaks around 4.0.
- **Bid:** the large chance (0.325) that the value is 0 makes high bids costly. Expected profit is about 0.08 at 1.0, 0.14 at 0.5, 0.15 at 0.3 and 0.16 at 0.1 to 0.0. It is roughly flat between 0.0 and 0.2.

I quote a bid of 0.2 and an ask of 4.0.

| Die 2 | Probability | Expected minimum |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.1 | 0 |
| 3 | 0.3 | 2.0 |
| 4 | 0.2 | 2.375 |
| 5 | 0.4 | 2.75 |

The weighted expected minimum is about **2.18**.

**Settlement distribution.**

| Settlement value | 0 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.325 | 0.225 | 0.225 | 0.075 | 0.15 |

**Bid side.** Informed traders sell to me whenever the value is 0, which happens 32.5% of the time. Noise traders sell when their valuation falls below my bid. Edge per quote:
- Bid 1.0: about +0.08
- Bid 0.8: about +0.107
- Bid 0.6: about +0.109

The best bid is about **0.7**.

- Ask 3.5: about +0.107
- Ask 3.8: about +0.126
- Ask 4.0: about +0.133
- Ask 4.2: about +0.131
