info.raw:
Expected settlement value with nothing revealed:
- **Die 2 = 0:** the minimum is 0.
- **Die 2 = 3:** E[min] = 16/8 = 2.
- **Die 2 = 4:** E[min] = 19/8 = 2.375.
- **Die 2 = 5:** E[min] = 22/8 = 2.75.

So the fair value is 0.3·2 + 0.2·2.375 + 0.4·2.75 = **2.175**.

The settlement value is spread out. About 32.5% of the time it is 0, and it can also be 4 or 5. Informed traders will hurt a tight quote, so I quote roughly ±1.1 around fair value.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 3.3}

Expected settlement value with nothing revealed:

- **Die 2 = 0** (prob 0.1): the minimum is 0.
- **Die 2 = 3** (prob 0.3): the mean of min(die 1, 3) is 16/8 = 2.0.
- **Die 2 = 4** (prob 0.2): the mean of min(die 1, 4) is 19/8 = 2.375.
- **Die 2 = 5** (prob 0.4): the mean of min(die 1, 5) is 22/8 = 2.75.

So the fair value is 0.6 + 0.475 + 1.1 = 2.175.

The settlement value is 0 with probability 0.325, so an informed seller is a real risk on the bid side. On the ask side, an informed buyer appears when the value is 4 or more, which has probability 0.225. The no-trade at 1.1 / 3.3 tells us little.

I'll keep a wide spread around 2.175, slightly tighter on the ask.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 3.2}

Die 2 = 3, so the contract settles at min(die 1, 3). The possible values are 0, 2 or 3.

**Fair value.** From die 1 alone, the outcomes are 0 (2/8), 2 (2/8) and 3 (4/8), which gives a mean of 2.0. The stage-1 history shifts this slightly:
- **Quote 1 (no trade at 1.1 / 3.3):** an informed trader with value 0 would have sold at 1.1. So no trade makes value 0 a little less likely.
- **Quote 2 (they bought at 3.2):** an informed trader can never value the contract above 3.2, so this buyer was a noise trader. It tells us nothing about die 1.

The posterior is about 13% for 0, 29% for 2 and 58% for 3, so fair value is about 2.31.

**Ask.** The maximum settlement value is 3, so any ask at or above 3 cannot be lifted by an informed trader. Only noise traders buy there. Expected edge is (ask − 2.31) × P(noise valuation > ask), which peaks around 3.6.

**Bid.** At any bid at or below 2, informed traders only sell when the value is 0. That costs about 0.35 × 0.13 × bid. Against that, I collect edge on noise sellers. Bids of 0.8 to 1.0 give the best net, about +0.15 per quote.

{"bid": 0.9, "ask": 3.6}

Die 2 = 3, so the contract settles at min(die 1, 3).

**Settlement distribution**
- Die 1 faces 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 10 give settlement values 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3.
- So the value is 0 with probability 1/4, 2 with probability 1/4, and 3 with probability 1/2.
- Fair value is 16/8 = 2.0. I treat this as the noise traders' centre.

**Ask side**
- Any ask at or above 3 can never be lifted by an informed trader, since the value is at most 3.
- Expected profit from noise buyers is 0.65 × P(noise > ask − 2) × (ask − 2):
  - Ask 3.0: about 0.188.
  - Ask 3.3: about 0.199.
  - Ask 3.4: about 0.199.
  - Ask 3.5: about 0.197.
- An ask of 2.9 does worse, about 0.163, because informed traders buy whenever the value is 3.
- I'll quote ask 3.4.

**Bid side**
- Any bid above 0 is hit by informed traders whenever the value is 0, losing the bid amount.
- A bid of exactly 0 cannot be hit by informed traders, because the value is never below 0.
- Expected profit at bid 0.0 is 0.65 × P(noise < −2) × 2 ≈ 0.65 × 0.133 × 2 ≈ 0.173.
- That beats bid 0.5 (about 0.153), bid 0.9 (about 0.115) and bid −0.3 (about 0.150).
- I'll quote bid 0.0.

Either trade keeps my position within the −3 to +3 limit.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Before any flips are revealed, the fair value is 4.5.

- **Fair value:** With probability ½ the coin is fair, giving an expected 3 heads. With probability ½ it always lands heads, giving 6. So the average is 0.5 × 3 + 0.5 × 6 = 4.5.
- **Risk on the ask:** Half the time the true value is exactly 6. An informed trader would then buy at any ask below 6. So I keep the ask fairly high, at 5.6, which limits that loss to 0.4 per trade.
- **Risk on the bid:** In the fair-coin case the value is spread around 3. An informed trader would sell to me whenever the value is below my bid. A bid of 3.3 keeps most of that exposure small.
- **Noise traders:** Their valuations spread with a standard deviation of 2.6. That is wide enough that both 3.3 and 5.6 should still attract noise trades, which is where I make money.

{"bid": 3.3, "ask": 5.6}

Before any flips are revealed, the contract is worth about 4.91 after one buy at 5.6. I'll quote a bid of 3.1 and an ask of 6.8, both set well away from fair value to limit losses to an informed trader.

**Prior value.** The coin is either fair or two-headed, each with probability 1/2.
- If it is two-headed, the contract settles at 6.
- If it is fair, it settles at Binomial(6, 0.5), which averages 3 and can also be 6.
- So P(settle = 6) ≈ 0.5 + 0.5/64 ≈ 0.508, and the prior expected value is 4.5.

**Update from the buy at 5.6.**
- An informed counterparty only buys at 5.6 if the value is 6.
- A noise trader buys if 4.5 + noise > 5.6, which happens with probability about 0.336.
- If the value is 6, the chance of a buy is 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.336 ≈ 0.469. Otherwise it is 0.8 × 0.336 ≈ 0.269.
- So P(value = 6) rises to about 0.643.
- If the value is not 6, its expected value is about 2.95.
- The new public fair value is 0.643 × 6 + 0.357 × 2.95 ≈ **4.91**.

**Choosing the quote.** I compared expected profit across ask levels and bid levels.
- **Ask:** for any ask of 5 or higher, an informed buyer only buys if the value is 6. Setting the ask at 6 or above removes that loss entirely. Expected profit then rises with the ask and is roughly flat between 6.6 and 7, so I pick 6.8.
- **Bid:** an informed seller sells whenever the value is below my bid. The fair-coin outcomes sit around 2 to 4, so a bid near 3 limits that loss. Expected profit peaks around 2.9 to 3.0.
- I am short 1, so buying back a unit helps, and I nudge the bid up slightly to 3.1.

{"bid": 3.1, "ask": 6.8}

Two heads in a row make the always-heads coin more likely, and the stage-1 buy at 5.6 pushes that further. I estimate public fair value at about **5.75**.

**Posterior after flips 1 and 2 are heads:**
- The chance of two heads is 1/4 for the fair coin and 1 for the always-heads coin, so P(always-heads) = 0.8.
- The expected count from the remaining 4 flips is 0.8 × 4 + 0.2 × 2 = 3.6.
- Expected settlement is therefore 2 + 3.6 = 5.6.

**Effect of the stage-1 buy at 5.6:**
- An informed trader buys at 5.6 only if settlement is 6.
- A noise trader valuing around the stage-1 fair value of 4.5 buys about 34% of the time.
- So the buy is about 0.47 likely if settlement is 6, versus about 0.27 otherwise.
- Updating on this gives P(settlement = 6) ≈ 0.88.
- Otherwise the coin is fair and settlement averages about 3.87.
- Combined, the public fair value is about 0.88 × 6 + 0.12 × 3.87 ≈ 5.75.

**Ask at 6.0:**
- Settlement cannot exceed 6, so an informed trader never buys there.
- Any fill comes from a noise trader and earns about 0.25 per unit on average.

**Bid at 4.9:**
- A noise trader sells there about 37% of the time, about 0.85 below fair value.
- An informed trader sells only when settlement is 4 or less, which has low probability.
- Buying also reduces my short position of -1.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.0}

The public fair value is about 5.6. My ask sits above the maximum possible settlement, so it can only lose to noise traders. My bid sits far enough below fair value to keep losses to informed sellers small.

**Fair value**
- Two heads give a posterior P(biased coin) = 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.5·0.25) = 0.8.
- If the coin is biased, settlement is 6.
- If it is fair, settlement is 2 + Bin(4, 0.5), with mean 4.
- Expected value = 0.8·6 + 0.2·4 = 5.6.
- The buy at 6 in quote 3 carries no information. Settlement can never exceed 6, so an informed trader would not buy there.

**Ask**
- Any ask above 6 can only be hit by noise traders, so every sale there is a guaranteed profit.
- Expected profit per quote is 0.8 × P(noise > ask − 5.6) × (ask − 5.6). It peaks at about 0.35 near an ask of 7.5.
- Going one unit shorter, to −3, is safe because any sale above 6 cannot lose.

**Bid**
- An informed trader sells only if settlement is below my bid. That needs the fair coin plus low flips, so the chance is small.
- At a bid around 3.5–4, the expected gain from noise sellers is about 0.34–0.35. The expected loss to informed sellers is only about 0.01–0.015.
- A buy also reduces my short position.

{"bid": 3.8, "ask": 7.5}

With four heads in a row, the coin is very likely the always-heads one. I'm quoting wide around a fair value of about 5.94, with the ask well above 6.

**Fair value**
- The chance the coin is fair, given 4 heads, is (½·1/16) / (½·1/16 + ½) = 1/17.
- The expected settlement is 4 + (16/17)·2 + (1/17)·1 ≈ 5.94.
- The settlement value is 6 with probability about 0.956, 5 with about 0.029, and 4 with about 0.015.
- Earlier trades give little information, so the public fair value stays at about 5.94.

**Ask**
- An informed trader values the contract at 6 or less, so it never buys at an ask of 6 or above. Only noise traders do.
- The expected gain is 0.8 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 5.94). This is largest at an ask of about 8: for example, 0.8 × 0.21 × 2.06 ≈ 0.35.
- Going from −2 to −3 is acceptable because every sale above 6 is profitable in every outcome.

**Bid**
- An informed trader would sell only if the true value is below my bid. At a bid of 4.0 that never happens, since the value is at least 4.
- For noise traders, the expected gain is P(valuation < bid) × (5.94 − bid). This peaks at a bid of about 4.0: 0.227 × 1.94 ≈ 0.44.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.9}

With four heads revealed, the coin is almost certainly the always-heads one. My estimate of fair value is about 5.94, and both quotes sit about 1.95 from it.

**Which coin it is**
- If the coin is fair, four heads in a row has probability 1/16.
- Given four heads, P(fair) = (½ × 1/16) / (½ × 1/16 + ½) = 1/17.

**Expected settlement**
- With the always-heads coin (16/17), settlement is 6.
- With the fair coin (1/17), settlement is 4 + Bin(2, 0.5), so it averages 5.
- Expected value = 16/17 × 6 + 1/17 × 5 ≈ 5.94.
- Settlement is 6 with probability about 95.6%, 5 with about 2.9%, and 4 with about 1.5%.

**Quote placement**
- **Ask:** An ask at or above 6 cannot be lifted by an informed trader, because settlement never exceeds 6. Against noise traders, the ask that maximises expected profit is about fair + 0.75σ ≈ 5.94 + 1.95, which gives about 7.9.
- **Bid:** The same reasoning gives a bid of about 5.94 − 1.95 ≈ 4.0. An informed trader would only sell if the value were below 4, which cannot happen.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.9}

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 5.9}

The public fair value is about **4.95** after the first trade, so I'll post a bid of 3.6 and an ask of 6.0.

- Before any trades, the settlement value is 6 with probability about 0.508. That covers the always-heads coin plus the 1-in-64 chance the fair coin shows all heads. Otherwise the fair coin gives a mean of about 2.95.
- The first counterparty bought at 5.9. An informed trader buys there only if the value is 6. A noise trader buys there with probability about 0.30.
- So a buy is more likely when the value is 6 (0.436 versus 0.236). This raises P(value = 6) to about 0.656.
- Fair value ≈ 0.656 × 6 + 0.344 × 2.95 ≈ **4.95**.

**Ask at 6.0**
- The settlement value can never exceed 6, so an informed trader will never buy from me there.
- Only noise traders lift it, about 34% of the time, and each such sale earns about 1.05 over fair value.

**Bid at 3.6**
- Noise traders sell to me about 30% of the time, at roughly 1.35 below fair value. That is worth about +0.32 per quote.

{"bid": 3.6, "ask": 6.0}

Fair value after two heads is about 5.6.

- **Which coin:** two heads are 4 times as likely with the biased coin (1 vs 0.25). So P(biased coin) = 1 / 1.25 = 0.8.
- **Expected settlement:** the 2 revealed heads plus 4 more flips. That gives 2 + 0.8×4 + 0.2×2 = 5.6.
- **Ask at 6.0:** the settlement cannot be higher than 6, so an informed trader never buys at 6.0. Only noise traders buy there, and each sale earns about 0.4 against fair value.
- **Bid at 4.9:** an informed trader sells to me only if the coin is fair and the final count is 4 or lower, which is fairly rare. Noise traders sell often enough for the 0.7 edge per trade to outweigh that risk.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.0}

Fair value is about 5.6, so I quote 3.5 / 7.5, roughly 2 either side of it.

**Fair value.** Two heads raise P(always-heads coin) from 1/2 to 0.8, so P(fair coin) = 0.2.
- The 4 unrevealed flips are expected to give 0.8×4 + 0.2×2 = 3.6 more heads.
- Fair value ≈ 2 + 3.6 = 5.6.
- The settlement is 6 with probability ≈ 0.81. It falls to 2–5 only if the coin is fair.

**Ask.** An informed trader who knows the value is 6 never buys at an ask of 6 or higher, so above 6 I only trade with noise traders.
- I estimated expected profit per quote at several asks: about 0.26 at 6.5, 0.33 at 7, 0.35 at 7.5 and 0.34 at 8.
- 7.5 is the best of these.

**Bid.** An informed trader sells to me only if the value is below my bid, which can only happen with the fair coin.
- After subtracting expected losses to informed sellers, expected profit is about 0.27 at a bid of 4.5, 0.33 at 4, 0.35 at 3.5 and 0.33 at 3.
- 3.5 is the best of these.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 7.5}

With four heads in a row the coin is very likely the biased one, so I quote wide and centred near 5.94.

**Fair value**
- Four heads: the chance the coin is biased is (1/2·1)/(1/2·1 + 1/2·1/16) = 16/17.
- Expected settlement: 4 + (16/17)·2 + (1/17)·1 ≈ **5.94**.
- The settlement is 6 with probability about 0.956. It cannot exceed 6.

**Ask**
- An informed trader values the contract at 6 at most, so any ask of 6.0 or higher is never hit by informed flow.
- The ask only faces noise traders, whose valuation is about N(5.94, 2.6).
- Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 5.94):

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 7.5 | 0.34 |
| 8.0 | 0.35 |
| 8.5 | 0.33 |

- The best is about **8.0**. Selling more is low-risk because the value is close to known.

**Bid**
- An informed trader sells only if the true value (4 or 5) is strictly below my bid. Those cases are rare (about 4%).
- Against noise traders, a bid of 4.0 gives about 0.8 × 0.23 × 1.94 ≈ 0.35.
- A bid of exactly 4.0 is not hit by an informed trader whose value is 4.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 8.0}

Four heads in a row make the two-headed coin very likely. Here are the numbers:

- **Posterior:** P(two-headed coin) = 1 / (1 + 1/16) = 16/17.
- **Expected settlement:** 4 + (16/17)·2 + (1/17)·1 ≈ 5.94.
- **Settlement distribution:** 6 with probability ≈ 0.956, 5 with ≈ 0.029, 4 with ≈ 0.015.

**Ask:** An informed trader only buys if the settlement value is above my ask. With an ask of 6 or more, that never happens. So the ask only trades with noise traders, and I want to maximise x·P(noise > x), where x is the ask minus fair value. For normal noise with standard deviation 2.6, the best markup is about 0.61σ, roughly 1.6. That puts the ask at about 7.5.

**Bid:** On the bid side, informed traders sell only if the value is 4 (or 5 when the bid is above 5). Both are rare. The same calculation for noise sellers puts the bid about 1.6 below fair, at about 4.3.

{"bid": 4.3, "ask": 7.5}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Quoting **bid 2.8, ask 6.0**: the ask risks nothing to informed traders, and the low bid limits what they can take.

**Fair value.** Each coin type has probability 1/2.
- Biased coin (always heads): 6 heads.
- Fair coin: Binomial(6, 0.5), which averages 3 heads.
- Expected settlement = 0.5·6 + 0.5·3 = 4.5.

The settlement is about 6 with probability ≈0.51 and otherwise spread roughly 0–5, centred at 3.

**Ask side.** The settlement can never exceed 6. An ask of 6.0 therefore loses nothing to informed traders, since they only buy when their value is above the ask. Noise traders (4.5 ± 1.7) buy at 6.0 about 19% of the time, gaining about 1.5 each.
- Expected edge per quote ≈ 0.65 · 0.19 · 1.5 ≈ +0.18.
- A lower ask such as 5.0 or 5.5 does worse, because informed traders would buy whenever the coin is the biased one.

**Bid side.** A bid between 2.5 and 3.0 balances the two effects:
- Informed sellers act when the fair coin produced few heads, costing about 0.05–0.08 per quote.
- Noise sellers trade at an edge of about 1.5–2, gaining about 0.16–0.18 per quote.
- Net is about +0.10 per quote anywhere in this range; I'll use 2.8.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 6.0}

Before any flips, the fair value is 4.5: half the time the coin is two-headed and settles at 6, otherwise it averages 3. The last quote (2.8 / 6.0) didn't trade, which tells us almost nothing.

**Ask side**
- An informed buyer arrives with probability 0.35 and lifts the ask whenever settlement is 6. Settlement is 6 with probability about 0.508.
- Each 0.1 that the ask sits below 6 therefore costs about 0.018 in expected value.
- Noise buyers pay well above fair value.
- My rough estimates of expected profit per quote:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 5.5 | about +0.09 |
| 5.8 | about +0.15 |
| 5.9 | about +0.17 |
| 6.0 | about +0.18 |

- The peak is around 5.9–6.0. I chose 5.9 since it is within about 0.02 of the 6.0 estimate.

**Bid side**
- Informed sellers hit the bid only when settlement is below it, which requires the fair coin plus a low head count.
- Expected profit:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 2.8 | about +0.105 |
| 3.0 | about +0.10 |
| 3.5 | about +0.04 |

- I chose 3.0, which is essentially as good as 2.8 and gets more noise sellers.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 5.9}

Bid 2.8, ask 6.0. These maximise expected profit given who might trade with me.

**Fair value.** The two coin types are equally likely, so fair value is 0.5 × 3 (fair coin) + 0.5 × 6 (two-headed coin) = 4.5. The settlement is about 6 with probability about 0.508, which comes from the two-headed coin plus the fair coin showing all heads. The rest follows a fair-coin binomial weighted by ½:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | 0.508 |
| 5 | 0.047 |
| 4 | 0.117 |
| 3 | 0.156 |
| 2 | 0.117 |
| 1 | 0.047 |
| 0 | 0.008 |

The two earlier quotes drew no trades, which tells me very little.

**Ask side.**
- Any ask below 6 loses to informed traders whenever the coin is two-headed.
- At 5.9, expected profit is about +0.17.
- At 6.0, no settlement value is above the ask, so informed traders never buy. Expected profit from noise traders is about 0.65 × 0.19 × 1.5 ≈ +0.18, which is the best I found.
- At 6.2 it drops to about +0.176, because fewer noise traders buy.

**Bid side.** Expected profit is about +0.10 to +0.106 anywhere from 2.5 to 3.0, with 2.8 slightly the best. Informed traders sell only when the settlement is 2 or lower, and that loss is outweighed by gains from noise sellers.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 6.0}

The first two flips were both tails, so the coin must be the fair one: the biased coin always lands heads. The contract settles at the number of heads in flips 3 to 6, which is Binomial(4, 0.5). That has a mean of 2 and a standard deviation of 1.

**Choosing the ask.** If I sell at ask a, I lose to informed traders (probability 0.35) whenever the true value is above a. I gain from noise traders (probability 0.65) whenever their valuation, 2 + N(0, 1.7), is above a. Expected profit per quote:

| Ask | Informed loss | Noise gain | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.5 | 0.077 | 0.125 | 0.048 |
| 3.0 | 0.022 | 0.181 | 0.159 |
| 3.2 | 0.018 | 0.187 | 0.170 |
| 3.4 | 0.013 | 0.187 | **0.174** |
| 3.5 | 0.011 | 0.184 | 0.173 |

The best ask is about 3.4. The value distribution is symmetric around 2, so the best bid is about 0.6.

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 3.4}

The coin is now known to be fair, since a biased coin always lands heads and flip 1 came up tails. Flips 1–2 contributed 0 heads, so settlement is the number of heads in the 4 remaining fair flips. That is Binomial(4, 0.5): mean 2, standard deviation 1, with probabilities 1/16, 4/16, 6/16, 4/16, 1/16 for 0 to 4 heads.

**Choosing the ask.** I compared expected profit per quote for several asks. Noise traders value the contract at 2 + N(0, 1.7), so they buy with probability P(Z > (ask − 2)/1.7). Informed traders buy only when the true value is above the ask.

| Ask | Noise buys | Gain from noise | Loss to informed | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.9 | 29.8% | 0.174 | −0.033 | 0.141 |
| 3.0 | 27.8% | 0.181 | −0.022 | 0.159 |
| 3.2 | 24.0% | 0.187 | −0.018 | 0.170 |
| 3.3 | 22.2% | 0.188 | −0.015 | 0.172 |
| 3.4 | 20.5% | 0.187 | −0.013 | 0.174 |
| 3.5 | 18.9% | 0.184 | −0.011 | 0.173 |

The best ask is about 3.4. The distribution is symmetric around 2, so the best bid is about 0.6. My position is flat, so there is no reason to skew. I'll keep the same quote as last time.

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 3.4}

The first two flips were tails, so the coin must be the fair one. The two revealed flips add 0 heads, so the value is just the heads in the 4 remaining flips. That is Binomial(4, 0.5): mean 2, standard deviation 1, range 0 to 4.

For the ask, I compared expected profit per quote at several prices. Noise traders buy with probability P(2 + N(0, 1.7) > ask) and give me ask − 2. Informed traders only buy when the value is above my ask, and they cost me the difference.

| Ask | Informed loss | Noise gain | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.0 | 0.022 | 0.181 | 0.159 |
| 3.3 | 0.015 | 0.188 | 0.172 |
| 3.4 | 0.013 | 0.187 | 0.174 |
| 3.5 | 0.011 | 0.184 | 0.173 |

An ask of 2.9 is clearly worse (net about 0.14), because a value of 3 then also hurts me. The best ask is about 3.4. The distribution is symmetric around 2, so the matching bid is 0.6. My position is flat, so I don't need to skew the quotes.

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 3.4}

Flips 1 and 2 were tails, so the coin must be the fair one.

**Settlement value**
- 2 heads are already showing, and flips 5 and 6 are fair.
- So settlement is 2 + Binomial(2, 0.5): it is 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25.
- Fair value is 3.

**Choosing the spread**
- If my bid is below 2 and my ask is above 4, an informed trader never trades with me. That removes all adverse selection.
- Noise traders' valuations are centred on 3 with standard deviation 1.7.
- I compared symmetric quotes around 3:
  - 1.9 / 4.1: expected edge about 0.37 per quote
  - 1.7 / 4.3: expected edge about 0.375 per quote
  - 1.5 / 4.5: expected edge about 0.37 per quote
- 1.7 / 4.3 is the best of these.
- My position of +1 leaves room to trade on either side.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

The coin must be the fair one, because tails appeared (a coin with P(heads) = 1 never shows tails).

**Settlement value**
- 2 heads are already fixed from flips 3 and 4.
- Flips 5 and 6 are fair coin flips.
- So the settlement value is 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4. The public fair value is 3.

**Informed traders**
- They know the value is between 2 and 4.
- A bid below 2 or an ask above 4 can never be hit by an informed trader.

**Noise traders**
- Their valuation is 3 + N(0, 1.7).
- Let x be the distance from 3 to my quote. Expected profit per side is 0.65·x·P(N > x).
- This is largest at about x ≈ 1.28·σ/1.7 scale, which gives x ≈ 1.3.

So I quote bid 1.7 and ask 4.3. This is safe from informed traders and earns the most from noise traders. My position of +1 doesn't constrain this.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

With flips 1 and 2 both tails, the coin must be the fair one, since a coin with P(heads) = 1 never shows tails.

**Settlement value**
- Two heads are already revealed (flips 3 and 4).
- Flips 5 and 6 are fair, so the remaining heads follow Bin(2, 0.5).
- Settlement is 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4.
- The public fair value is 3.

**Informed traders**
The maximum possible settlement is 4. If my ask is at or above 4, an informed trader never buys from me at a loss to me. By symmetry, a bid at or below 2 avoids losing to an informed seller.

**Noise traders**
Expected profit on the ask side from noise buyers is 0.65 × P(N(0, 1.7) > a − 3) × (a − 3):

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 4.0 | ≈ 0.181 |
| 4.3 | ≈ 0.188 |
| 4.4 | ≈ 0.187 |
| 4.5 | ≈ 0.184 |

An ask below 4 (e.g. 3.9) does worse: it earns less from noise traders and also loses to informed buyers when settlement is 4.

So the best ask is about 4.3, and by symmetry the best bid is 1.7. A buy would take my position from +2 to +3, which is within the limit.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The contract's fair value before anything is revealed is **4.5**: it is 6 if the coin is double-headed, otherwise an average of 3 heads, and each coin has probability 1/2.

The settlement value is lopsided:
- It equals 6 about 51% of the time, from the double-headed coin plus all-heads with the fair coin.
- Otherwise it is spread out like a fair-coin count of heads, from 0 to 6.

**Ask side.** Informed traders buy above my ask only when the value is 6, so an ask a bit above 5 limits that loss. Noise traders value the contract at 4.5 ± 1.7. At an ask of 5.5, about 28% of them buy, and I gain about 1 per unit against fair value.

**Bid side.** Informed traders sell below a bid around 3.3 only when the value is 3 or less. That happens about 33% of the time, with an average value near 2.2, so I lose about 1.1 per unit. Noise traders sell with probability about 24%, and I gain about 1.2 per unit.

Both sides have positive expected profit, so I quote both.

{"bid": 3.3, "ask": 5.5}

Fair value is about 3.56 after the sale at 3.3. I'm quoting roughly 0.9–1.0 either side of that, skewed slightly down because I'm long.

**Prior.** The settlement value V is the number of heads in 6 flips.
- With probability 1/2 the coin is fair, so V follows a Binomial(6, 0.5).
- With probability 1/2 the coin always lands heads, so V = 6.
- That gives P(V=k), in 128ths, for k = 0…6: 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 65.
- The prior mean is 4.5.

**Update from the sale at 3.3.** A counterparty sells to me when its valuation is below my bid.
- An informed trader (probability 0.35) sells only if V ≤ 3.
- A noise trader (probability 0.65) sells if 4.5 + noise < 3.3. That happens with probability Φ(−1.2/1.7) ≈ 0.24.
- So the chance of this sale is about 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.24 ≈ 0.506 if V ≤ 3.
- It is about 0.65 × 0.24 ≈ 0.156 if V ≥ 4.

**Posterior.** Weighting each value by its prior probability and the chance of the sale gives a posterior mean of about 3.56. The posterior is still two-humped: about 29% of the weight is on V = 6, and the rest leans towards lower values.

**Quote.** I bid 2.7 and offer at 4.6.
- The spread is wide because 35% of counterparties know V exactly and V is spread widely.
- Both prices sit a little lower than a centred quote, so I am less likely to buy again and more likely to sell, since I'm already long 1.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 4.6}

Fair value is about 3.44, so I'm quoting **bid 2.4 / ask 4.3**.

**Prior.** With probability 1/2 the coin is fair, giving a Binomial(6, 0.5) count with mean 3. With probability 1/2 it is double-headed, giving 6 heads. The prior mean is 4.5.

**Quote 1 (they sold at 3.3).** An informed trader sells only if the settlement value is 3 or less. A noise trader sells about 24% of the time.
- For a value of 3 or less, the chance of this sale is 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.24 ≈ 0.51.
- For a value of 4 or more, it is about 0.16.
- After this update, the expected value falls to about 3.56.

**Quote 2 (no trade at 2.7 / 4.6).** An informed trader does nothing only if the value is 3 or 4. A noise trader does nothing about 42% of the time.
- Values 3 and 4 now carry about 0.63 likelihood; all other values carry about 0.28.

**Posterior.** The chances are now:

| Settlement value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 3 | ~45% |
| 6 | ~20% |
| 2 | ~15% |
| 4 | ~10.5% |
| Other values | small |

That puts fair value around 3.44.

**Quote.** I centre the quote slightly below fair value because I'm already long one unit.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 4.3}

After flips 1 and 2 both came up heads, the coin alone would point to about 80% biased. The stage-1 trading history pulls that down a lot, so I put fair value near 4.25.

**Without the history:** P(biased | HH) = 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.125) = 0.8. Expected value = 0.8 × 6 + 0.2 × (2 + 2) = 5.6.

**Adding the history:** I worked out how likely the three stage-1 outcomes are under each case. I used a stage-1 public fair value of 4.5 for the noise traders.

| Quote | Outcome | Noise-trader probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Counterparty sold at 3.3 | 0.156 |
| 2 | No trade (2.7 / 4.6) | 0.247 |
| 3 | No trade (2.4 / 4.3) | 0.224 |

- **Biased coin (value 6):** an informed trader would have bought at quotes 2 and 3. Only a noise trader explains all three outcomes, so the likelihood is about 0.156 × 0.247 × 0.224 ≈ 0.0086.
- **Fair coin:** settlement is 2 + Binomial(4, 0.5). A settlement of 3 fits the history best, since an informed trader would sell at 3.3 and then not trade. A settlement of 4 also fits fairly well. Weighting by the binomial probabilities gives a likelihood of about 0.068.
- **Posterior:** P(biased) = (4 × 0.0086) / (4 × 0.0086 + 0.068) ≈ 0.34.
- **Expected value if fair:** about 3.36, given the history.
- **Expected value overall:** 0.34 × 6 + 0.66 × 3.36 ≈ **4.25**.

The value is bimodal: about 6 if the coin is biased, about 3 to 4 if it is fair. I'll quote a fairly wide spread around 4.25. Being long 1 already, I lean slightly toward selling.

{"bid": 3.6, "ask": 5.0}

Fair value is about 5.3. I'm bidding 4.4 and asking 6.0.

**Coin type after two heads.** The prior is 1/2 fair and 1/2 two-headed. Two heads have probability 1/4 under a fair coin and 1 under a two-headed coin. So P(fair) = 0.125 / (0.125 + 0.5) = 0.2, and P(two-headed) = 0.8.

**Settlement value before quote 4.** The two revealed heads count 2. The remaining 4 flips add 4 if the coin is two-headed and 2 on average if fair. So E = 2 + 0.8 × 4 + 0.2 × 2 = 5.6.

**Effect of no trade at quote 4 (3.6 / 5.0).** If the coin is two-headed, the value is 6. An informed trader would then have bought at 5.0, so the only way to get no trade is a noise trader valuing between 3.6 and 5.0. That has probability about 0.16. If the coin is fair, values of 4 or 5 also produce no trade from an informed trader, which happens often. Updating on this gives P(two-headed) ≈ 0.63. Given a fair coin, the expected value is about 4.2. So fair value is now about 0.63 × 6 + 0.37 × 4.2 ≈ 5.3.

**Ask.** The maximum settlement is 6, so an ask of 6.0 can never be lifted by an informed trader. Noise traders centred on 5.3 still buy above 6 about a third of the time, which is pure edge.

**Bid.** At 4.4 the bid is about 0.9 below fair value. That leaves room for informed sellers when the coin is fair and the value is low. A fill would only take me to +2, well within the position limit.

{"bid": 4.4, "ask": 6.0}

Fair value is about **5.1**. I'm quoting bid **4.2** / ask **5.8**, about 0.9 below and 0.7 above fair value, slightly skewed toward selling because I'm already long 2.

**Fair value from the two revealed heads.**
- Two heads are 4 times as likely with the always-heads coin as with the fair coin (1 vs 1/4), so P(always-heads coin) = 0.8.
- The 4 unrevealed flips are expected to give 0.8×4 + 0.2×2 = 3.6 more heads, for a total of 2 + 3.6 = 5.6.

**Adjusting for the sale at 4.4 on quote 5.**
- An informed trader sells at 4.4 only if the true total is 4 or less, which requires the fair coin.
- A noise trader sells at 4.4 with probability P(Z < −1.2/1.7) ≈ 0.24.
- So a sale at 4.4 has probability 0.35 + 0.65×0.24 ≈ 0.51 if the total is 4 or less, and 0.65×0.24 ≈ 0.16 otherwise.
- Re-weighting the possible totals by these chances lowers fair value to about 5.1. P(total = 6) is now roughly 0.62; otherwise the total is most likely 4 or below.

**Choosing the quote.**
- Ask 5.8: an informed buyer only takes it when the total is 6, and then I lose just 0.2.
- Bid 4.2: an informed seller only hits it when the total is 4 or less.

{"bid": 4.2, "ask": 5.8}

The coin must be the fair one, because flips 3 and 4 came up tails and the always-heads coin can't produce a tail. That gives 2 heads so far, with 2 fair flips left. Settlement is 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4, so fair value is 3.

**Ask:** An informed trader only hurts me if settlement is 4 and my ask is below 4. Noise traders value the contract at 3 plus noise with standard deviation 1.7. Expected profit per quote on the ask side is about:
- 0.08 at an ask of 3.5
- 0.15 at 3.8
- 0.18 at 4.0
- 0.19 at 4.2 (the peak)
- 0.18 at 4.5

**Bid:** The bid side is symmetric. An informed seller only appears if settlement is 2 and my bid is above 2. Bids between about 1.8 and 2.0 earn roughly 0.18–0.19 per quote.

Being long 3 doesn't change expected profit, so I quote close to symmetric and stay just inside the peaks, at 1.9 and 4.1.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 4.1}

Two tails have been revealed, so the coin must be the fair one. Heads so far are 2, and the last two flips are fair. Settlement is therefore 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities ¼, ½, ¼, so fair value is 3.

**Ask:**
- If I ask above 4, informed traders never buy, because the most the contract can settle at is 4.
- Expected profit from noise buyers is about 0.65 × P(noise > a) × (a − 3).
- That is roughly 0.185 at 4.1, 0.188 at 4.3 and 0.184 at 4.5, so about 4.3 is best.

**Bid:**
- By symmetry, I bid below 2, so informed traders never sell to me.
- 1.7 earns the same expected profit as 4.3 on the ask side.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

The fair value is 3, and the best quotes are a bid of 1.7 and an ask of 4.3.

**Fair value.** Flips 3 and 4 came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one (the other coin always lands heads). Two heads are already in. Flips 5 and 6 add 0, 1 or 2 more heads with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25. So settlement is 2, 3 or 4, with an expected value of 3. The coin is now known, so the trading history adds no further information.

**Ask side.** Take an ask of 3 + x, with x of at least 1 so the ask is 4 or higher.
- An informed buyer never buys, because settlement is at most 4.
- A noise trader buys if their valuation is above the ask, which happens with probability 1 − Φ(x/1.7).
- Each such sale earns x on average, so expected profit is 0.65 × (1 − Φ(x/1.7)) × x.

Trying a few values of x:

| x | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | ≈ 0.181 |
| 1.2 | ≈ 0.187 |
| 1.3 | ≈ 0.188 (peak) |
| 1.5 | ≈ 0.184 |

So the ask is about 4.3.

**Bid side.** The problem is symmetric around 3, so the bid is about 1.7. An informed seller never sells there, because settlement is at least 2.

**Position.** Since I'm maximising expected profit, my current long position of +3 doesn't change these quotes.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

| Value | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.02 | 0.12 | 0.30 | 0.10 | 0.08 | 0.03 | 0.34 |

- At 5.5 the expected profit is about +0.10.
- At 5.8 it is about +0.11.
- At 6 it is about +0.12.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 5.7}

Flip 2 came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one (a coin with P(heads) = 1 never shows tails). The two remaining hidden flips are not what pins the value: flips 3–6 are all fair and still unknown to the public.

- Possible values are 1 to 5, with probabilities 1/16, 4/16, 6/16, 4/16, 1/16.
- The public fair value is 3.

**Ask level**
An informed trader buys only when the value is above my ask. A noise trader buys with probability P(fair + noise > ask), where the noise has standard deviation 1.7. The expected profit per quote on the ask side is:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|-----|-----------------|
| 3.6 | about +0.07 |
| 4.1 | about +0.17 |
| 4.3 to 4.5 | about +0.17 (the peak) |

**Bid level**
The bid side is symmetric around 3, so the best bid is about 1.6. I am long 1, but that is small, so I keep the quote roughly symmetric.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 4.4}

The second revealed flip was tails (flip 2 = 0), which only the fair coin can produce, so the coin is fair. The settlement value is therefore 1 plus a Binomial(4, 0.5) count. Its expected value is 3, and the possible values run from 1 to 5 with probabilities 1/16, 4/16, 6/16, 4/16, 1/16.

**Choosing the ask.** The expected profit of each ask balances two things: gains from noise traders, whose valuations are 3 plus noise with standard deviation 1.7, and losses to informed traders, who buy only when the true value is above the ask.

| Ask | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.5 | 0.65 × 0.384 × 0.5 = 0.125 | 0.35 × (0.25×0.5 + 0.0625×1.5) = 0.077 | ≈ 0.05 |
| 4.0 | 0.65 × 0.278 × 1.0 = 0.181 | 0.35 × 0.0625 × 1.0 = 0.022 | ≈ 0.16 |
| 4.4 | 0.65 × 0.205 × 1.4 = 0.187 | 0.35 × 0.0625 × 0.6 = 0.013 | ≈ 0.174 (best) |
| 4.5 | 0.65 × 0.189 × 1.5 = 0.184 | 0.35 × 0.0625 × 0.5 = 0.011 | ≈ 0.173 |
| 4.9 | 0.65 × 0.132 × 1.9 = 0.163 | 0.35 × 0.0625 × 0.1 = 0.002 | ≈ 0.16 |

**Choosing the bid.** The value distribution is symmetric around 3, so the best bid mirrors the ask at 1.6. My current position of +1 is well inside the ±4 limit, so it doesn't push the quote in either direction.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 4.4}

Flips 2–4 came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one (the always-heads coin can't land tails). Flips 5 and 6 are each 50/50. That means settlement = 1 + Binomial(2, 0.5):

| Settlement | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 1/4 | 1/2 | 1/4 |

So the fair value is 2.

**Informed traders** know the settlement exactly, so it is always 1, 2 or 3. If my ask is at least 3, an informed trader never buys, because they only buy when their value is strictly above my ask. Likewise, a bid at or below 1 means they never sell to me.

**Noise traders** value the contract at 2 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 1.7. On the ask side my expected profit is 0.65 × P(noise > a − 2) × (a − 2):
- a = 3.0: about 0.181
- a = 3.3: about 0.188
- a = 3.5: about 0.184
- a = 4.0: about 0.156

The best ask is about 3.3. The problem is symmetric around 2, so the matching bid is 0.7. My position of +1 is well inside the limits, so I don't need to skew the quotes.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.3}

This is the last quote, so I just maximise the expected profit on this one trade.

**Settlement value.** Flips 2–4 came up tails, which rules out the always-heads coin, so the coin is fair. One head has shown so far, and flips 5 and 6 are fair. The settlement is therefore 1, 2 or 3 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25. The fair value is 2.

**Ask side.**
- Any ask of 3 or more cannot lose to an informed trader. The value is at most 3, and they only buy if their valuation is strictly above my ask.
- An ask between 2 and 3 loses to an informed buyer when the value is 3. Checking the derivative of expected profit shows it is still rising at an ask of 3, so the best ask is at or above 3.
- From 3 upward, only noise traders buy. Writing x for the ask minus 2, expected profit is 0.65 × x × P(noise > x), with noise standard deviation 1.7. This peaks at about x = 1.28.
- An ask of 3.3 (x = 1.3) gives about 0.65 × 1.3 × 0.222 ≈ 0.19. An ask of 3.0 gives about 0.18.

**Bid side.** The value distribution is symmetric around 2, so the same reasoning gives a bid of 0.7. My position is +1, so neither trade breaks the ±4 limit.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The contract's expected value is 4.5. It settles at 6 with probability about 0.51, which happens if the coin is two-headed or a fair coin lands all heads. Otherwise it follows a Binomial(6, ½) distribution.

**Ask:**
- An ask just below 6 is lifted by informed traders whenever the value is 6. That costs about (6 − ask) × 0.51 × 0.35 per quote.
- Noise traders value the contract at 4.5 plus noise with standard deviation 1.7. An ask near 6 still catches enough of them for an expected gain of roughly 0.19 per quote.
- An ask of 5.9 gives about the best balance: a small informed loss against nearly the full noise gain.

**Bid:**
- Informed traders sell only when the value is below my bid. With a fair coin, low outcomes have little probability.
- A bid around 2.8 gives the best balance:
  - Expected informed loss is about 0.07 per quote.
  - Expected noise gain is about 0.175 per quote.
  - Net edge is about +0.10.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 5.9}

Quote: **bid 2.5, ask 5.9**.

**Prior.** Half the time the coin is fair, so the settlement averages 3. Half the time it always lands heads, so it settles at 6. The starting fair value is therefore 4.5.

**Update from the no-trade at 2.8 / 5.9.** An informed trader holding a value of 6 would have bought at 5.9. No trade therefore makes the always-heads coin less likely. Working through the probabilities moves P(always-heads) down to about 0.39. The public fair value drops to about 4.3.

**Ask.** If the coin is always-heads, informed traders buy and I lose about 6 minus my ask. Noise traders buying above fair value pay me the ask minus 4.3. The expected edge is about 0.12 at 5.5, 0.15 at 5.7 and 0.17 at 5.9. At 6.0 it is about the same as at 5.9, so I'm keeping the ask at 5.9.

**Bid.** Informed traders sell when the true value is below my bid. With a fair coin, a value of 2 or less happens about a third of the time. The expected edge is about 0.09 at a bid of 3.0. At 2.5 it is about 0.10, because the informed losses get smaller faster than the noise profit does. So I'm lowering the bid to 2.5.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 5.9}

Flip 1 came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one (the other coin always lands heads). With flip 2 = 1 and four fair flips left, the settlement value is 1 + Binomial(4, 0.5). Its expected value is 3, and it ranges from 1 to 5, with P(5) = P(1) = 1/16.

**Choosing the spread.** I quote symmetrically, 3 ± a, and weigh two effects:
- **Informed traders (35%)** only trade against me when the true value is past my price. Pushing the ask above 4 means they only buy when the value is 5, and even then my loss is small.
- **Noise traders (65%)** have valuations of 3 + N(0, 1.7). The wider my spread, the more I earn per trade but the fewer of them trade.

**Expected profit per side for each half-spread a:**

| a | Ask side profit |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | 0.159 |
| 1.2 | 0.170 |
| 1.4 | 0.174 |
| 1.5 | 0.173 |

The best value is a = 1.4, giving a bid of 1.6 and an ask of 4.4.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 4.4}

Flip 1 came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one. That makes settlement = 1 + Bin(4, 0.5), with probabilities 1/16, 4/16, 6/16, 4/16, 1/16 for values 1 to 5. Before any trading the fair value is 3.

**Update from the last trade.** Someone bought at 4.4.
- An informed trader would only do that if the value is 5.
- A noise trader buys there with probability about 0.20.
- Folding this in moves the posterior fair value to about 3.28. It also raises the chance that the value is 5 to about 0.2.

**Ask side.**
- Any ask above 4 can only lose to an informed trader when the value is 5.
- Raising the ask gives up some noise buyers but earns a bigger margin on each.
- Expected profit levels off around an ask of 4.8–4.9, at about +0.17 per quote.

**Bid side.**
- A bid at 3 or higher gets hit by informed sellers when the value is 1 or 2. That loses money on average.
- A bid of 2.0 only loses to informed sellers when the value is 1, which is rare. Noise sellers still give about +0.17 per quote.
- Buying also reduces my short position, which is a small extra benefit.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 4.9}

The coin must be the fair one, since tails has appeared and the always-heads coin can never show tails.

**Fair value**
- Heads so far: 1.
- Flips 5 and 6 are fair, so the settlement is 1 + Bin(2, 0.5).
- That gives values 1, 2 and 3 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25.
- The fair value is 2.

**Choosing the ask**
- An informed trader buys only if the settlement value is above my ask. With an ask of 3.0 or more, that never happens.
- At or above 3.0, my expected profit comes only from noise traders. Noise traders value the contract at 2 plus normal noise with standard deviation 1.7.
- Expected profit per quote is 0.65 × (ask − 2) × P(noise valuation above the ask).
- This peaks at about 0.188 for an ask of 3.3:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 2.9 | 0.165 (includes a small informed loss) |
| 3.0 | 0.181 |
| 3.2 | 0.187 |
| 3.3 | 0.188 |
| 3.5 | 0.184 |

**Choosing the bid**
- The value distribution is symmetric around 2, so the same reasoning gives a bid of 0.7.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.3}

The last two revealed flips are tails, so the coin must be the fair one. One head has shown so far. The two hidden flips are fair, so settlement is 1 + Binomial(2, 0.5). That gives 1, 2 or 3 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25, so fair value is 2.

My position is 0 and this is the last quote, so I only need the quote that earns the most on this one trade.

**Ask side.** The informed trader can't buy from me at an ask of 3 or more, because settlement is at most 3. A noise trader buys at ask a = 2 + x with probability 1 − Φ(x/1.7), and I make x. Expected profit is 0.65·x·(1 − Φ(x/1.7)):
- x = 1.2: 0.187
- x = 1.3: 0.188 (highest)
- x = 1.4: 0.187

**Bid side.** The game is symmetric around 2, so the bid's best value is x = 1.3 below fair value.

That gives a bid of 0.7 and an ask of 3.3.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The quote is wide because informed traders' value is lopsided: half the time the contract settles at exactly 6, otherwise around 3.

**Fair value.** With probability 1/2 the coin is fair, so heads follow Binomial(6, 0.5) with mean 3. With probability 1/2 it always lands heads, giving 6. The expected settlement is 0.5·3 + 0.5·6 = **4.5**.

**Ask.** An informed trader buys at 5.5 whenever the value is 6, which happens just over half the time. At 6.0 an informed trader never buys at a loss to me, because the value can't exceed 6. Noise traders still buy about 12.5% of the time, earning me 1.5 each, so the edge is about +0.12 per quote. That beats 5.5 (about +0.05) and 6.2 (about +0.10).

**Bid.**
- **3.5:** roughly break-even. Informed sellers with values of 0–3 cost about as much as noise sellers earn.
- **3.0:** informed traders sell only when the value is 2 or less, about 17% of the time, with an average value of about 1.64. That costs about 0.08 per quote. Noise sellers earn about 0.12. The net edge is about +0.04.
- **2.5:** slightly worse, at about +0.03.

I'll quote a bid of 3.0 and an ask of 6.0.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

Fair value is about 4.6 after the quiet first quote. I'll quote a bid of 3 and an ask of 6.

**Fair value.** The coin is fair or always-heads with equal prior. A fair coin gives 3 expected heads out of 6, and an always-heads coin gives exactly 6. So the prior fair value is 4.5.

**Update from quote 1 (3 / 6, no trade).**
- If the coin is always-heads, an informed trader values the contract at 6. That is not above my ask of 6, so it never trades. Noise traders (sd 1.3 around 4.5) stay inside 3 to 6 about 75% of the time. So P(no trade) ≈ 0.84.
- If the coin is fair, an informed trader sells whenever the outcome is 2 or fewer heads (about 34% of the time). So P(no trade) ≈ 0.72.
- The posterior that the coin is always-heads rises to about 0.54. Fair value becomes about 3 + 3 × 0.54 ≈ 4.6.

**Ask.** Any ask below 6 loses money to informed buyers when the coin is always-heads. At 6, those buyers never trade, and noise buyers still lift the offer about 14.5% of the time. They pay about 1.4 above fair value, so the ask side earns roughly +0.13 per quote.

**Bid.** At 3, informed sellers with a fair coin cost about 0.075 per quote. Noise sellers earn about 0.11. That nets roughly +0.035, which beats bids of 2.5 or 3.5.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

The settlement value is either a fair-coin count or exactly 6, each with probability 1/2. So the prior fair value is 0.5×3 + 0.5×6 = 4.5, and there is a large point mass at 6 (about 0.51).

**Ask side:** An informed trader only buys above my ask when the value is 6. An ask just under 6 costs little against them. Noise traders, centred on about 4.5, still buy roughly 14% of the time at a profit of about 1.4. An ask of 5.9 gives about +0.11 expected profit, the best of the levels I checked.

**Bid side:** At a bid of 3, informed traders sell only when the value is 2 or less, which has probability about 0.17. Noise sells at that level still leave a positive edge of about +0.04. A higher bid, around 3.5, brings in too much informed selling at values of 3 or less.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 5.9}

Two heads make the biased coin likely, so I quote a low bid and an ask of 6.0.

**Posterior on the coin.** Two heads are 0.5 × 0.25 = 0.125 likely under a fair coin and 0.5 × 1 = 0.5 under the biased coin. So P(biased) = 0.5 / 0.625 = 0.8.

**Fair value.**
- Biased coin (0.8): the remaining 4 flips are all heads, so settlement is 6.
- Fair coin (0.2): settlement is 2 + Bin(4, 0.5), which is 4 on average.
- Expected settlement is 0.8 × 6 + 0.2 × 4 = **5.6**.

**Ask.** Settlement can never exceed 6. An informed trader buys only if its valuation is strictly above my ask, so at 6.0 it never buys. A noise trader still buys about 38% of the time, so 6.0 carries no adverse selection.

**Bid.** If the coin is fair, an informed trader values the contract between 2 and 5.
- I want a bid low enough to avoid most informed sells but high enough to catch noise sellers.
- I checked the expected edge per counterparty at bids of 5.2, 5.0, 4.8, 4.5 and 4.2. It peaks at about 4.2–4.5, roughly +0.1.
- I pick 4.4. Being short 1 also makes buying a unit welcome.

{"bid": 4.4, "ask": 6.0}

Fair value is about 5.81, so I quote bid 5.2 and ask 6.0.

**Posterior after the reveal.** Two heads in two flips is 4 times more likely with the biased coin (likelihood 1) than the fair coin (1/4). So P(biased) = 0.8.
- The expected value is 2 + 4 × (0.8 × 1 + 0.2 × 0.5) = 5.6.

**Update from the buy at 6 on quote 4.**
- If the value is 6, a buyer at 6 comes from the informed trader (0.35) or a noise trader (0.65 × 0.379). That gives a buy probability of about 0.596.
- If the value is below 6, only a noise trader buys, with probability about 0.246.
- Before the trade, P(value = 6) = 0.8 + 0.2/16 = 0.8125.
- After the trade, P(value = 6) is about 0.913.
- In the other outcomes the value averages about 3.87 (58/15).
- Fair value is therefore about 0.913 × 6 + 0.087 × 3.87 ≈ 5.81.

**Quote.**
- **Ask at 6.0:** an informed trader never buys at this price, because the value cannot exceed 6. A sale at 6 never loses money, and it gains in the non-all-heads cases.
- **Bid at 5.2:** this buys from noise sellers at a good edge, about +0.13 expected per quote. Informed sellers only hit it in the roughly 9% of cases where the value is 5 or less, costing about 0.04. Buying here also reduces the short position.

{"bid": 5.2, "ask": 6.0}

Posterior fair value is about 5.86, and the maximum possible settlement is 6.

**Fair value from the revealed flips**
- Two heads give P(biased coin) = 1 / (1 + 1/4) = 0.8.
- E[settlement] = 2 + 4 × (0.8 × 1 + 0.2 × 0.5) = 5.6.

**What the trading history adds**
- At quote 5, my bid was 5.2 and my ask was 6, and nobody traded.
- An informed trader with value 6 never trades there, because buying at 6 needs a value above 6.
- An informed trader with value 5 or less would have sold at 5.2.
- So the quiet quote is evidence for value 6. After updating, P(value = 6) ≈ 0.93, which gives fair ≈ 5.86.

**Ask side**
- An ask of 6.1 can never be lifted by an informed trader, since no settlement value exceeds 6.
- Any noise trader who buys pays above fair value, so every fill there is profitable.

**Bid side**
- A bid of 5.6 is below fair value. Noise sellers there are profitable.
- Adverse selection is small: only about 0.35 × 0.07 of arrivals are informed traders holding a low value.
- I am short 2, so buying back below 6 also cuts my risk if the coin is biased.

{"bid": 5.6, "ask": 6.1}

The contract will very likely settle at 6, so I'll quote a bid just below fair value and set the ask exactly at 6, where an informed buyer won't trade.

**Fair value.** Four heads in a row make the biased coin much more likely.
- The chance of four heads is 1/16 with the fair coin and 1 with the biased coin.
- So P(fair coin) = (½ × 1/16) / (½ × 1/16 + ½) = 1/17, and P(biased coin) = 16/17.
- Expected settlement = 4 + (1/17)(1) + (16/17)(2) ≈ **5.94**.

**Distribution of the settlement value:**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | ≈ 0.956 |
| 5 | ≈ 0.029 |
| 4 | ≈ 0.015 |

**Ask at 6.0.** An informed trader values the contract at 6 nearly every time. A buyer only trades if its valuation is above my ask, so an informed trader never buys from me at 6.0. A noise trader buys at 6.0 about 48% of the time, and I sell at a small edge over 5.94. That trade would take me to -4, which is still allowed.

**Bid at 5.8.** A noise trader sells to me about 46% of the time, giving me about 0.14 of edge per unit. It also reduces my short position. An informed trader sells only when the value is 5 or less, which happens about 4.4% of the time. Bidding 5.8 rather than 5.9 gives up a little volume but keeps more edge per trade and limits those informed-seller losses.

{"bid": 5.8, "ask": 6.0}

Four heads in four flips makes the fair coin very unlikely, so the fair value is just under 6.

**Posterior on the coin**
- P(4 heads | fair coin) = 1/16, and P(4 heads | two-headed coin) = 1.
- So P(fair) = (½·1/16) / (½·1/16 + ½) = 1/17.

**Fair value**
- Expected heads in flips 5–6 = 2·(16/17·1 + 1/17·0.5) ≈ 1.94.
- Fair value ≈ 4 + 1.94 = 5.94.

**Settlement distribution**
- 6 with probability about 95.6%.
- 5 with probability about 2.9%.
- 4 with probability about 1.5%.

**Ask at 6.0**
- An informed trader values the contract at 6 at most, so it never buys above 6.0.
- Only noise traders lift the offer, with each sale gaining about 0.06 on average.
- Selling one more unit takes me from -3 to -4, which is within the limit.

**Bid at 5.8**
- Noise traders sell to me about 46% of the time, gaining about 0.14 each.
- I only lose when an informed trader knows the value is 4 or 5, which has probability about 4.4%.
- Net expected value of the bid is slightly positive.

{"bid": 5.8, "ask": 6.0}

**Fair value.** Four heads from four flips makes the biased coin very likely.
- Chance of seeing four heads: (1/16) for the fair coin and 1 for the biased coin.
- Posterior probability the coin is fair = (1/2 × 1/16) / (1/2 × 1/16 + 1/2 × 1) = 1/17.
- Expected settlement = 4 + (16/17)×2 + (1/17)×1 ≈ 5.94.

**Settlement distribution.**

| Settlement value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | ≈ 0.956 |
| 5 | ≈ 0.029 |
| 4 | ≈ 0.015 |

**Bid choice.** Only the bid can be posted this quote, since my ask is pulled at -4.
- A noise trader sells to me if 5.94 + noise < bid, and I gain 5.94 − bid on that trade.
- An informed trader sells only if the true value is below my bid, which is a loss for me.
- Expected profit at each bid:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 5.9 | about −0.006 |
| 5.5 | about +0.09 |
| 5.1 | about +0.134 |
| 4.9 | about +0.139 |
| 4.7 | about +0.133 |

The best bid is around 4.9 to 5.0, so I bid 4.9.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": null}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Prior fair value is 0.5 × 6 + 0.5 × 3 = 4.5, since a fair coin averages 3 heads and a two-headed coin gives 6.

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only if the settlement value is above my ask, and the value can never exceed 6.
- At an ask of 6.0, informed traders never buy.
- Noise traders buy when their noise exceeds +1.5, which happens about 12% of the time.
- Expected edge on the ask is about +0.12, which is the best of the asks I checked.

**Bid side.** Selling informed traders come from the fair-coin case, where the value is usually around 3 and can be as low as 0.
- At a bid of 3.5, noise profit is about +0.14 and informed losses are about −0.14, so the edge is roughly zero.
- At a bid of 3.0, noise profit is about +0.12 and informed losses are about −0.08, giving about +0.04.
- At a bid of 2.5, the edge is about +0.03, so 3.0 is the best.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

The posterior fair value is about 3.27, so I'm quoting bid 2.2 and ask 4.2.

**Prior:** With probability 1/2 the coin is fair and the expected count is 3. With probability 1/2 it is two-headed and the count is 6. So the prior mean is 4.5.

**Update from the sell at 3:**
- An informed trader sells at 3 only if the settlement value is below 3. That means 0, 1 or 2 heads with the fair coin, which has probability 22/128 ≈ 0.17.
- A noise trader sells at 3 with probability P(4.5 + N(0, 1.3) < 3) ≈ 0.12.
- So the chance of a sell is 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.12 ≈ 0.43 if the value is below 3, and 0.65 × 0.12 ≈ 0.08 otherwise.

**Posterior:**
- Given the value is below 3, its mean is about 1.64. Given it is 3 or more, its mean is about 5.10.
- Weighting the two branches by prior probability times likelihood gives a posterior mean of about 3.27.

**Quote:** I keep the spread wide, because the value is bimodal and informed traders hurt badly on both sides. I skew slightly lower because I'm already long 1.

{"bid": 2.2, "ask": 4.2}

Fair value is now about 2.3. Two sells to me have pushed the estimate well below the prior of 4.5, so I am quoting around 2.3 with the ask set further out to cover the chance the coin always lands heads.

**Prior.** With probability 1/2 the coin always lands heads, so the contract settles at 6. Otherwise it is Binomial(6, 0.5). Settlement probabilities are about:
- 0: 0.008
- 1: 0.047
- 2: 0.117
- 3: 0.156
- 4: 0.117
- 5: 0.047
- 6: 0.508

The prior mean is 4.5.

**Updating on the two sells.** A counterparty who knows the value is 6 never sells, so each sell makes a low settlement more likely.
- **Sell at 3.** A seller who knows the value sells if S < 3. A noise trader sells with probability 0.65·Φ((3−4.5)/1.3) ≈ 0.081. The posterior mean becomes about 3.28.
- **Sell at 2.2.** A seller who knows the value sells if S ≤ 2. A noise trader sells with probability 0.65·Φ((2.2−3.28)/1.3) ≈ 0.132. The posterior mean becomes about 2.32.

The posterior is bimodal: P(S ≤ 2) ≈ 0.78 and P(S = 6) ≈ 0.12.

**Ask.** Any ask below 6 loses to an informed buyer when S = 6, so the ask must sit well above 2.3.
- At 3.0 the expected value is slightly negative.
- At 3.5 to 4.0 it is about +0.02.

I chose 3.5. Being hit there also reduces my long position of +2.

**Bid.** The losses to informed sellers come only from settlements of 0 and 1.
- At 1.5 the expected value is about +0.08.
- At 1.2 it is about +0.11.
- At 1.0 it is about +0.12.

I chose 1.1, leaning slightly lower because I am already long 2.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 3.5}

After flips 1 and 2 both came up heads, the flips alone put P(biased coin) at 0.8. The stage-1 trades shift this. Two sells at low bids (3 and 2.2) are more likely if an informed trader knew the fair coin would give a low total. The buy at 3.5 points the other way. Weighing these roughly, P(biased) comes out near 0.7.

- **If the coin is biased,** the contract settles at 6.
- **If the coin is fair,** the expected settlement is about 3.1.

So my estimate of fair value is about 5.1. The outcome is lopsided: most likely 6, otherwise a low value.

**Ask:** An informed trader buys whenever the value is 6, which is likely. A low ask would lose money on those trades, so I set the ask just under 6.

**Bid:** I set the bid somewhat below fair value. Informed traders will sell to me mainly in the fair-coin case. Noise traders give me some trades, and my long position of +1 is comfortable.

{"bid": 4.4, "ask": 5.9}

Here I quote 5.3 bid / 6.0 ask around an estimated fair value of about 5.81.

**Before quote 4's trade.** Flips 1 and 2 were both heads.
- Chance the coin is the always-heads one: 0.5×1 / (0.5×1 + 0.5×0.25) = 0.8.
- Expected heads in flips 3–6: 0.8×4 + 0.2×2 = 3.6.
- So the public fair value was 2 + 3.6 = 5.6.

**Updating on the buy at 5.9 in quote 4.**
- An informed trader buys at 5.9 only if the settlement value is 6.
- Chance the value is 6: 0.8 + 0.2 × (1/16) = 0.8125.
- A noise trader buys if their valuation is above 5.9. That happens with probability P(Z > 0.23) ≈ 0.41.
- Chance of that buy if the value is 6: 0.35 + 0.65×0.41 ≈ 0.62.
- Chance of that buy if the value is below 6: 0.65×0.41 ≈ 0.27.
- So the chance the value is 6, given the buy, is about 0.91.
- If the value is not 6, the coin is fair and the expected value is 58/15 ≈ 3.87.
- Updated fair value ≈ 0.91×6 + 0.09×3.87 ≈ 5.81.

**Quote.**
- **Ask 6.0:** Settlement can never be above 6, so informed traders never buy here. Only noise traders buy, which is pure edge.
- **Bid 5.3:** Noise traders sell at a price below fair, which gives edge. That gain outweighs the small risk (about 9%) that an informed trader sells because the coin is fair.

{"bid": 5.3, "ask": 6.0}

The posterior puts about 96% on the contract settling at 6, so fair value is roughly 5.93. I'll quote a bid of 5.5 and an ask of 6.0.

**Revealed flips.** Two heads are three times as likely under the always-heads coin as under the fair coin. That gives P(always-heads) = 0.8. Expected settlement is then 2 + 4×(0.8×1 + 0.2×0.5) = 5.6. P(settles at 6) = 0.8 + 0.2/16 ≈ 0.81.

**Trading history.**
- At quote 4, a counterparty bought at 5.9. An informed trader only does that if the settlement is 6. This moves P(settles at 6) to about 0.91.
- At quote 5, nobody traded with my bid at 5.3 and ask at 6. An informed trader would have sold at 5.3 if the settlement were 5 or less. If the settlement is 6, an informed trader does nothing at an ask of 6. This moves P(settles at 6) to about 0.96.

**Quote.**
- **Ask 6.0:** settlement cannot exceed 6, so selling at 6 never loses money. Only noise traders valuing it above 6 will buy.
- **Bid 5.5:** this sits a little below fair value. An informed trader sells only if settlement is 5 or less, which is about 4% likely. Noise traders sell below 5.5 often enough, about 37% of the time, to make the bid worth showing.

{"bid": 5.5, "ask": 6.0}

Four heads in four flips makes the biased (always-heads) coin very likely. The fair coin gives four heads with probability 1/16, so its posterior is about 1/17.

**Fair value:** the expected number of heads in the last two flips is 2 × 16/17 + 1 × 1/17, so the expected settlement is 4 + 33/17 ≈ 5.94. Settlement is 6 with probability about 0.96, 5 with about 0.03 and 4 with about 0.015.

**Ask:** an informed trader values the contract at no more than 6, so it never buys at an ask of 6 or higher. Above 6, only noise traders (5.94 plus noise with standard deviation 1.3) buy. Expected profit is 0.65 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 5.94). This peaks at about 0.14 per quote with an ask near 7.0.

**Bid:** informed traders sell only when the value is 5 or 4, which happens about 4% of the time. Weighing the noise-trader edge against that small informed loss, expected profit is about 0.14 per quote with a bid near 5.0.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 7.0}

Four heads in a row make the two-headed coin very likely. That puts fair value just under 6 and makes a settlement of 6 most likely.

**Posterior.**
- Fair coin: (1/2)(1/16) = 1/32. Two-headed coin: (1/2)(1) = 16/32.
- So P(fair coin) = 1/17 and P(two-headed coin) = 16/17.

**Settlement distribution.**
- 6 with probability about 0.956
- 5 with probability about 0.029
- 4 with probability about 0.015
- Fair value is 4 + 33/17 ≈ 5.94.

**Ask side.** Any ask below 6 is bought by the informed trader, who almost always knows it settles at 6. So the ask should sit at 6 or above, where only noise traders (value 5.94 ± 1.3) buy.

| Ask | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 6.0 | 0.65 × 0.48 × 0.06 ≈ 0.02 |
| 6.5 | 0.65 × 0.33 × 0.56 ≈ 0.12 |
| 7.0 | 0.65 × 0.21 × 1.06 ≈ 0.14 (best) |
| 7.5 | 0.65 × 0.115 × 1.56 ≈ 0.12 |

**Bid side.** At a bid of 5, a noise trader sells with probability about 0.235, earning about 0.94 each time, so about 0.144. The informed trader sells only if the value is 4, which costs about 0.005. Net is about 0.14.

Raising the bid to 5.5 is worse: noise profit drops to about 0.105, and informed sellers at values 5 and 4 cost about 0.013.

I'll quote a bid of 5 and an ask of 7.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 7.0}

Expected settlement value is about 5.94, so I'll quote wide on both sides: bid 4.9, ask 6.9.

**Updated belief about the coin.** Four heads in four flips is 1/16 as likely with the fair coin as with the always-heads coin. So the chance the coin is fair is (1/16) / (1 + 1/16) = 1/17.

**Expected settlement value.**
- Always-heads coin: settles at 6.
- Fair coin: 4 heads so far plus 1 expected from the last two flips, so 5.
- Combined: E = 6 − 1/17 ≈ 5.94.
- By outcome, settlement is 6 with probability ≈ 65/68, 5 with probability ≈ 2/68, and 4 with probability ≈ 1/68.

**Ask.**
- An informed trader values the contract at 6 at most, so any ask above 6 is never hit by them.
- Against noise traders, the edge is x·P(noise > x), where x is how far the ask sits above 5.94 and noise has standard deviation 1.3. This peaks at x ≈ 1.0, so the ask is about 6.9.
- Expected edge there is about 0.96 × 0.23 ≈ 0.22.

**Bid.**
- At 4.9 the edge against noise traders is about 1.04 × P(Z < −0.8) ≈ 0.22.
- An informed trader would sell at 4.9 only if the settlement were 4 or less. That happens with probability ≈ 1/68, so it costs very little.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.3 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 1/10, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The coin's expected heads probability is 0.4×0.3 + 0.1×0.4 + 0.5×0.9 = 0.61. That gives a fair value of 8 × 0.61 × 10 = 48.8.

The settlement value is bimodal:
- **Low cluster:** about 24 ± 13, if it is the 0.3 coin.
- **High cluster:** about 72 ± 8.5, if it is the 0.9 coin.

Either way, an informed trader's valuation sits roughly 23–25 away from 48.8, so a narrow spread would be picked off on most informed arrivals. I estimated the expected profit per quote for a few half-spreads, setting gains from noise traders against losses to informed traders:

| Half-spread | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 15 | about 5.5 | about 3.5 | about 2 |
| 20 | about 5.7 | about 2.1 | about 3.6 |
| 25 | about 5.5 | about 1.2 | about 4.3 |
| 30 | about 4.8 | about 0.7 | about 4.1 |

A half-spread of about 25–26 does best, which puts the quotes near 23 and 75.

{"bid": 23, "ask": 75}

Fair value works out to about 33 after the first trade.

**Prior.** The coin's expected heads probability is 0.4·0.3 + 0.1·0.4 + 0.5·0.9 = 0.61. Over 8 flips that gives an expected settlement of 80 × 0.61 ≈ 48.8.

**What the sale at 23 tells us.**
- An informed trader sells at 23 only if settlement is below 23, which means at most 2 heads.
- The chance of at most 2 heads is about 0.25. In that case the expected settlement is about 14.6.
- A noise trader sells at 23 with probability about 0.16, since its noise must fall below −25.8.
- Weighting the two cases gives an informed share of about 0.088 and a noise share of about 0.105.
- The posterior fair value is (0.088 × 14.6 + 0.105 × 48.8) / 0.193 ≈ 33.

**Quote.** The settlement value is very spread out and 35% of counterparties are informed, so I keep the spread wide. I lean slightly lower because I am already long one unit.

{"bid": 14, "ask": 50}

Bid 48, ask 66.

**Fair value.** Flips 1–4 show 3 heads and 1 tail. Updating the prior on that gives these posterior probabilities for the coin:

| P(heads) | Posterior probability |
|---|---|
| 0.3 | ≈ 0.158 |
| 0.4 | ≈ 0.080 |
| 0.9 | ≈ 0.762 |

- The expected P(heads) is about 0.765.
- So the 4 remaining flips should give about 3.06 heads.
- Adding the 3 heads already seen, fair value is about 60.6.

The two stage‑1 sells were at 23 and 14. With 3 heads already showing, settlement is at least 30, so neither seller could have been informed. Those sells give no information now.

**Settlement distribution.** The outcome is lumpy:
- With the 0.9 coin, settlement is mostly 70 (≈66% chance) or 60.
- With the low‑bias coins (0.3 or 0.4), it is around 40–50.

**Quote.** Informed traders will lift any ask below 70 and hit any bid above about 50. I want the spread wide enough to limit that adverse selection while still trading with noise traders, whose standard deviation is 26. I am long 2, so I skew the quote slightly down to encourage selling to me less and buying from me more.

{"bid": 48, "ask": 66}

Fair value is about 60.6. I'm quoting bid 40 and ask 77, set wide to avoid losing to informed traders.

**Coin posterior after 3 heads and 1 tail:**

| Coin (P heads) | Weight | Posterior |
|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 0.0189 × 0.4 | 0.158 |
| 0.4 | 0.0384 × 0.1 | 0.080 |
| 0.9 | 0.0729 × 0.5 | 0.762 |

- The expected P(heads) is 0.765.
- Fair value is 30 + 40 × 0.765 ≈ 60.6.

**Settlement distribution** (4 flips left):

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 30 | 0.048 |
| 40 | 0.093 |
| 50 | 0.107 |
| 60 | 0.246 |
| 70 | 0.505 |

**Ask side:** About half the time the settlement is 70, so any ask below 70 sells to informed traders at a loss. The expected profit against noise traders (fair value plus noise with standard deviation 26) peaks with the ask around 75–85. Since I'm long 2, I lean slightly toward selling and put the ask at 77.

**Bid side:** A bid of 40 only loses to informed traders when settlement is 30, which has probability 0.048. It still captures enough noise sellers, so the expected value is about +2.7 per quote, roughly the best available.

{"bid": 40, "ask": 77}

Six of the eight flips are revealed. They show 5 heads and 1 tail, so the coin is almost certainly the 0.9 one.

**Which coin it is.** Weight each coin's prior by the chance of seeing 5 heads and 1 tail:
- 0.3 coin: about 2.2%
- 0.4 coin: about 2.0%
- 0.9 coin: about 95.8%

That gives an expected chance of heads of about 0.877 per remaining flip.

**Fair value.** The 5 heads so far are worth 50. The two remaining flips add 10 × 2 × 0.877, so fair value is about 67.5. The contract can only settle at 50, 60 or 70:
- 70 (both remaining flips heads): 78%
- 60 (one head): 19%
- 50 (no heads): 3%

**Ask.** An informed trader only buys if the true value is above my ask, so any ask of 70 or more is never hit by one. Only noise traders, valued around 67.5 ± 26, buy up there. Expected profit from them is highest around an ask of 85–90, so I use 86.

**Bid.** By the same logic, a bid of 50 or less is never hit by an informed trader, because the settlement is never below 50. Expected profit from noise traders selling to me is highest around 50.

{"bid": 50, "ask": 86}

Five of the six revealed flips are heads, so the 0.9 coin is very likely: its posterior probability is about 0.958. The expected head probability for each remaining flip is about 0.877.

**Fair value:** 50 + 2 × 10 × 0.877 ≈ 67.5.

**Possible settlements:**

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 50 | ≈ 0.028 |
| 60 | ≈ 0.191 |
| 70 | ≈ 0.781 |

**Ask:** Any ask at 70 or above can never be hit by an informed trader, because the most the contract can settle at is 70. Against noise traders (fair value plus noise with SD 26), expected profit (ask − 67.5) × P(valuation > ask) peaks at about 4.4 per noise trade, at an ask of about 87–88.

**Bid:** Any bid at 50 or below can never be hit by an informed trader, because the least the contract can settle at is 50. Against noise traders, expected profit (67.5 − bid) × P(valuation < bid) peaks at about 4.4 per noise trade, at a bid of 48–50. Bidding higher, such as 60, takes on informed losses in the 50-settlement case and lowers expected profit to about 1.9 per noise trade.

Buying one more unit would take the position to +3, which is within the limit.

{"bid": 15, "ask": 31}

Fair value after the reveals and last quote's trade is about 25.4, so I'm quoting 19 bid / 33 ask, roughly centred there.

|---|---|---|---|

Six flips are revealed with 2 heads. The contract settles at 20 + 10 × (heads in flips 7 and 8), so it can only settle at 20, 30 or 40.

- p = 0.4 → 0.19
- p = 0.9 → 0.004

This gives E[p] ≈ 0.32. Before using the trade history, the chances of 0, 1 or 2 more heads are about 0.46, 0.43 and 0.11. That makes fair value about 26.4.

- If the settlement is 20 or 30, it is about (0.65 × 0.45)² ≈ 0.086.

Updating on this gives roughly P(20) ≈ 0.33, P(30) ≈ 0.32 and P(40) ≈ 0.35. Fair value is therefore about 30.

**Quote:** I am short 2, so I set the quote around 30 with the ask skewed slightly higher. Bid 25 and ask 36 keep me profitable against informed traders at either extreme, 20 or 40. Noise traders, with a standard deviation of 26, will still trade at these prices.

- P(p = 0.9) ≈ 0

That gives E[p] ≈ 0.32. Two flips remain, so expected remaining heads ≈ 0.64. Fair value is therefore about 26.4.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 3/5, P(heads) = 0.8 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 24.8, and I'm quoting 20.8 bid / 28.8 ask: roughly ±4 around fair value to cover the risk of trading with informed counterparties.

- **Expected chance of heads per flip:** 0.6 × 0.5 + 0.4 × 0.8 = 0.62.
- **Expected settlement:** 5 × 8 × 0.62 = 24.8.
- **Uncertainty in the settlement value:**
  - If P(heads) = 0.5, the expected settlement is 20 with variance 50.
  - If P(heads) = 0.8, it is 32 with variance 32.
  - Not knowing which coin adds 0.24 × 12² = 34.56 to the variance.
  - Total variance is about 77, a standard deviation of about 8.8.
- **Spread:** an informed counterparty knows the exact value, which can sit well away from 24.8, so I need a buffer. Noise traders' valuations spread with standard deviation 6.6, so a spread of about ±4 still trades with a fair share of them.

{"bid": 20.8, "ask": 28.8}

The public fair value is the expected number of heads times 5.

- **Expected chance of heads:** 0.6 × 0.5 + 0.4 × 0.8 = 0.62.
- **Expected heads in 8 flips:** 8 × 0.62 = 4.96.
- **Fair value:** 5 × 4.96 = 24.8.

The quote-1 no-trade barely changes this, so fair value stays about 24.8.

The settlement value is spread widely, so an informed trader could profit a lot from a tight quote. Wide quotes cost little, because a noise trader's valuation is fair value ± 6.6 standard deviation, so many still trade. I'm narrowing slightly from last time to 3.5 on each side of fair value, to attract some noise flow.

{"bid": 21.3, "ask": 28.3}

- The expected chance of heads on each flip is 0.6 × 0.5 + 0.4 × 0.8 = 0.62.
- Over 8 flips that gives 4.96 expected heads, so the contract is worth 24.8.
- The standard deviation of the value is about 8.8.

- If the value is higher, only a noise trader sells, with probability about 0.24.
- The expected heads are about 3.2 in the low case and 6.2 in the high case.

The no-trade at quote 1 pulls the estimate slightly back toward the middle, giving about 22.8.

{"bid": 19.4, "ask": 26.0}

Fair value is about 22.7, so I'm quoting roughly ±3.5 around it: bid 19.2, ask 26.2.

{"bid": 19.2, "ask": 26.2}

Fair value is about 22.7, so I'm quoting roughly ±3 around it with a flat position.

- Fair coin: 0.6 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.150
- Biased coin: 0.4 × 0.2 × 0.8 = 0.064

{"bid": 19.7, "ask": 25.7}

Fair value is about 23, so I'll quote 20 bid and 26 ask, skewed slightly up because I'm short one unit.

- Prior: fair coin (p = 0.5) with probability 0.6, biased coin (p = 0.8) with probability 0.4.

- Posterior: P(fair) ≈ 0.70 and P(biased) ≈ 0.30.

- Biased coin: (2/5) × 0.8⁴ × 0.2³ = 0.00131

**Quote choice.**
- An informed trader sells only if the value is below my bid. With a bid of 20.0, they never sell.
- An informed trader buys only if the value is above my ask. With an ask of 25.0, they never buy.
- Noise traders still trade at about a 33–37% chance per side. The expected edge is about 2.2–2.8 per trade.
